El receptor venezolano habló sin filtros sobre su futuro incierto en Milwaukee, reconociendo que Yankees fue uno de los equipos mencionados en conversaciones de canje que, por ahora, no llegaron a nada.
William Contreras reveló en el podcast de Ronald Acuña Jr. que Yankees mostraron interés en adquirirlo, aunque "no salió nada de eso".
William Contreras decidió hablar abiertamente sobre su futuro con Cerveceros de Milwaukee, justo antes de la Serie Mundial 2026, donde el conjunto cervecero busca su primer título de la franquicia. En el podcast de Ronald Acuña Jr., el receptor venezolano confirmó que su nombre ya ha sonado en conversaciones de intercambio, y señaló específicamente a Yankees de Nueva York como uno de los equipos interesados.

"Tengo un año de arbitraje restante. Estamos cerca. Veremos. Con Milwaukee, no sé. Nunca se sabe. Tenemos a Quero, un prospecto de receptor. Esto es un negocio, nunca sabes dónde vas a aterrizar. Se mencionaron Yankees, uno de esos equipos grandes. Salió el tema un par de veces, pero no salió nada de eso", declaró Contreras.
¿Por qué Nueva York tiene sentido como destino?
La declaración del propio Contreras coincide con múltiples reportes recientes que ya lo vinculaban a los Yankees. Nueva York necesita con urgencia un receptor que mejore la producción ofensiva de Austin Wells, quien bateó apenas .186/.292/.332 con 14 jonrones esta temporada, muy por debajo de la línea de .270/.341/.417 con 18 cuadrangulares que Contreras dejó en 147 juegos de la fase regular. El propio Contreras hizo referencia a Jeferson Quero, el prospecto de receptor que Milwaukee desarrolla en su sistema, como parte de la ecuación que podría facilitar su salida si el equipo decide reemplazarlo internamente.
Pese a la lógica del encaje, hasta ahora todo se mantiene en el terreno especulativo: no hay confirmación de negociaciones activas, solo el reconocimiento del propio jugador de que el tema "salió un par de veces" en el radar de rumores.
William Contreras acknowledged that a trade could certainly happen this winter, even if the Brewers do end up winning the World Series. He mentioned the Yankees as one of the teams that’s called Milwaukee in prior seasons. Should the Yankees circle back? https://t.co/p4d3EAlyN7— Everything Yankees (@eyyankees)
October 27, 2026

Lo que respalda su valor en el mercado
Más allá de las conversaciones de canje, los números respaldan por qué William Contreras genera tanto interés. Según Spotrac, su valor de mercado actual se calcula en 86,368,686 de dólares por seis años, con un promedio anual de 14,394,781, cifras que reflejan su nivel como uno de los mejores receptores más completos del béisbol. El venezolano, de 28 años, es tres veces All-Star (2022, 2024, 2026) y dos veces ganador del Bate de Plata, consolidado como pieza clave detrás del plato para una rotación de Milwaukee que lo llevó hasta la cima de la Liga Nacional esta temporada.
Con apenas un año de contrato restante antes de la agencia libre, el futuro de William Contreras dependerá en gran medida de lo que decida Milwaukee una vez concluya la Serie Mundial: renovarlo, dejarlo llegar a su último año de arbitraje o, finalmente, abrir la puerta a un traspaso que equipos como Yankees seguirán de cerca.

¿Quién es William Contreras?
William Contreras nació el 24 de diciembre de 1997 en Puerto Cabello, Venezuela, y debutó en Grandes Ligas en 2020 con Bravos de Atlanta, equipo con el que fue campeón de Serie Mundial en 2021. Canjeado a Cerveceros de Milwaukee tras la temporada 2022, se consolidó como uno de los mejores receptores ofensivos de la Liga Nacional, ganando el Bate de Plata en 2023 y 2024.
Tres veces All-Star, hoy juega su primera Serie Mundial como titular absoluto detrás del plato con Milwaukee.

Who Is Brewers' World Series MVP? A-Rod, Jeter And Ortiz Make Their Picks
If the World Series ends on Tuesday night with the Milwaukee Brewers sweeping the Tampa Bay Rays? Kevin Burkhardt posed the question to Derek Jeter, Alex Rodriguez and David Ortiz ahead of Game 4, and while they all had different answers to the question, they eventually reached the same conclusion.
Jeter started by saying that the Brewers have played so much like a team that an individual MVP is almost beside the point. He compared it to the New England Patriots running out together for pregame introductions in Super Bowl XXVI in 2001.
"You might as well just give it all to the entire team with how they played," the five-time World Series champion said.
But under the pressure of having to choose one, Jeter went with William Contreras, the Brewers' super-charged catcher.
"I think what he’s done offensively, defensively, game calling, ABS challenges; he’s pretty much done all you could ask of from a catcher so far up until this point," Jeter said.
(Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images)
Rodriguez had a hard time disagreeing.
"He’s affecting both sides of the ball; he’s calling a great game; he’s consulting at the [end] of Game 2, when Pat Murphy asks, ‘Should I keep Ashby out there?’ and he says yes," Rodriguez said. "Heck, he’s also the best umpire in the league because last night he was again 4-for-4. The guy is like an A.I. robot."
Ortiz’s first answer was a hedge. He said picking one player was hard and listed three of them.
"That’s a tough one, Kevin, because everybody has been able to deposit something to win ball games," Ortiz said. "But I got to tell you, when you think about a guy like Ashby coming out of the bullpen, Contreras and Chourio, I mean, you can roll the dice with them, because all of them have done something special to win ball games."
After hearing Jeter and Rodriguez, Ortiz finally made a decision.
"I got Contreras, man," Ortiz said. "The Bazooka!"

ST. PETERSBURG — The Brewers won by a mile because they're obsessed with the inches.
Nobody would describe the final outcome of Milwaukee's emphatic beatdown on Monday — a 10-1 drubbing of the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 3 of the World Series — as "close." Not since 2015 has there been a larger margin of victory in a World Series game. The Brewers' 16-to-3 hit advantage over the flailing Rays was the third-largest in Fall Classic history. Starter Robert Gasser allowed just one one hit and faced the minimum across six brilliant innings, becoming the first lefty to do that in a World Series game since Sandy Koufax in 1965. A massive gathering of Brewers fans, an estimated 30% of the crowd, was there to witness it all, their voices joyously hoarse by the end.
It was a shellacking of historic proportions.
But Milwaukee's commanding 3-0 series lead, one that places this franchise on the precipice of its first championship, was earned in the margins on a bang-bang play that folks in the Badger State will remember for a long time.
Up a pair in the top of the fifth, the Brewers put runners on first and second against Tampa Bay starter Freddy Peralta. Milwaukee catcher William Contreras, the best hitter in these playoffs, ripped a two-hopper toward third baseman Junior Caminero. In a spinning motion, Tampa's talented talisman snagged the pearl and flicked it to second baseman Ben Williamson as a full-bore Christian Yelich slid into the bag. Umpire Dan Bellino punched his fist. The FOX graphic evaporated from the screen. Multiple members of Tampa Bay's between-innings hype squad jogged onto the outfield track for some type of giveaway.
Yelich, though, clung to the bag with his left hand as he motioned adamantly toward Belino with his right.
"Safe, safe."
Safe, indeed.
The Brewers challenged the call. Before Bellino could finish announcing the overturn, Tampa Bay skipper Kevin Cash was already headed toward the mound to pull Peralta.
But no move, at that point, could have stopped the inevitable.
"The whole game was changed when Yeli was safe at second," Brewer manager Pat Murphy insisted afterwards. "That's just a hustle play. When your leader makes that play, that says it all. The game was changed because he did a little thing that anybody can do."
Yelich, by beating the throw to second, turned a dead frame into the inning of a lifetime. The floodgates soon burst, sweeping away Tampa's next pitcher, Cam Booser. On a 2-2 count, he served a mid-zone fastball to second baseman Brice Turang, who scorched one off shortstop Taylor Walls' glove and into the outfield. Milwaukee's lead was doubled.
As the sizable traveling contingent — a bar down the street sold out of Miller Lite before first pitch — went berzerk, the Fox broadcast panned to a young Rays fan, who could be seen uttering to his companion a harsh and humbling realization: "That's the series."
Milwaukee, though, would leave no doubt. And then some.
Their next five batters all found grass, with each consequential hit eliciting louder and louder roars from the armada of traveling Wisconsinites. In total, the Brewers strung together seven consecutive two-out hits to plate eight two-out runs, a World Series record. It was an all-time heater and a fitting performance from a pridefully selfless Brewers offense that has prioritized passing the baton over hitting big flies all season long.
"Nobody wants to be the hero," hitting coach Dan Vogelbach boasted.
That might be true, but Yelich, with his mad dash to second, was the under-the-radar hero of this evening.
With the right-handed Contreras at the plate and a runner on second, Rays first baseman Ryan Villade was shaded toward second, opting not to hold Yelich on. That allowed the Brewers' captain to take a much larger-than-average lead off first base. By the time Contreras swung, Yelich was already about 30 feet from the bag, his right foot in the air ready to break in either direction. As the ball bounced toward Caminero, Yelich landed and broke hard for second.
"You have to understand where you're at in space," Yelich explained postgame. "You're lengthening your primary [lead] in case there's a ball in the hole or some sort of play happens where you could potentially beat the throw."
It was a sublime bit of baserunning, the kind that takes years of purposeful, monotonous practice to get good at. There's also an element of internal pre-pitch preparation: "If X happens, I do Y." Yelich executed that process perfectly. Caminero, who had ample time to get the slow-footed Contreras at first, did not.
"The beauty of it is that you have guys like Yeli that demand it from the group," first-base coach Spencer Allen told Yahoo Sports about the team's attention to detail.
Jason Lane, Milwaukee's offense and strategy coordinator, explained to Yahoo Sports that he tells players to approach a secondary lead at first base and two outs with the same intent and intensity they would bring to a "contact play." That's the inside-baseball term for when a runner at third, with the infield drawn in, plans to race home on contact — no matter where the ball's hit.
"When you remind guys of that and explain it to them like that — and these guys are hunting all those little things that we preach about right turns — it can become something that happens in a playoff game," he explained.
On a team that cares deeply about the little things, Yelich, the group's most accomplished character, might care most of all. That establishes a standard, one that has helped push the Brewers to an amazing 10-1 record this postseason. But that crucial play, and its outcome, was about more than Yelich's impressive read and instincts. His footspeed from first to second clocked in at 28.5 mph, a full tick faster than his season average. That's an 81st-percentile result from a 34-year-old DH with a history of back problems.
Yelich was once a speedster before age and injuries did their thing. There exists a timeline in which the 2018 MVP evolved into a bat-first baseclogger, a plodder focused on in-box responsibilities. Instead, Yelich has done everything in his power to remain as athletic, as lithe and as quick as possible. Years of treatment, offseason sprint work, healthy habits, weight room sessions — all of it has allowed Yelich to maintain his speed despite the barrage of injuries and his status as a primary DH.
"I've got some things that have happened to me, but for the most part, I feel pretty good," he said when asked about his speed. "I feel like I can still hang with the boys out there."
The boys agree.
"That baserunning by Yeli there, which allowed us to have that huge inning ..." outfielder Sal Frelick said. "We work on those things in spring. He's the guy that's running the meeting, saying this is important. It's his 14th season. He's been All-Star, Silver Slugger, MVP, and nobody cares about baserunning more than him. Just to see him do that, get a good secondary, run as hard as he could and beat that out — that's what allowed us to have that big inning."
"Little things like that — that's what makes our team great."
Great might be an understatement. If the Brewers finish the deal in Game 4, they would become the first team in the League Championship Series era to sweep both the championship series and World Series rounds. They would finish this month a mind-boggling 11-1, with their only defeat coming by one run in NLDS Game 3 in San Diego. There's a strong argument that we are currently witnessing the most dominant postseason team in MLB history.
The gap between these Brewers and the rest of the league is a massive chasm, yes, but it's one they chiseled one swing and one step at a time.

In recent years, the Milwaukee Brewers have traded away star players before they hit the open market, often eliciting a confusing reaction from most baseball fans.
However, it's those same fans who are shocked when the Brewers find themselves back atop the National League Central and in contention for a World Series. The Brewers formula is proving to work now better than ever, as they have the best record in baseball in the last two years and are two wins away from a championship.
If they win it all, the big question will be how strictly they stick to their formula. Corbin Burnes, Freddy Peralta, Devin Williams and Josh Hader were all traded with one eye on the future, and about a year before they hit the open market. After this year, the two Brewers' stars in the same situation are William Contreras and Trevor Megill.
An All-Star closer and an All-Star catcher who may be the best in baseball are sure to cost a fortune, at a price tag the Brewers won't like. However, this World Series run could change things slightly in Milwaukee.
"The Brewers believe they will have more money at their disposal after the World Series run, according to people who were familiar with the situation who were not authorized to speak publicly because the tally of the revenue had not been finalized. That could create more flexibility in spending on player salaries," wrote The Athletic's Andy McCullough and Will Sammon. "But a significant deviation from the organization’s roster-building model is unlikely, especially as the baseball operations department readies itself for whatever rule changes take place after the expiration of the current labor agreement Dec. 1."
The Brewers are not going to turn into the Los Angeles Dodgers or New York Mets overnight. However, they may be more open to making an exception to their rules for Contreras and Megill. Megill is very replaceable, especially with Abner Uribe and Aaron Ashby in-house. However, they would be losing a big part of their clubhouse.
Contreras is borderline irreplaceable with anyone in the organization right now, both on the field and in the clubhouse. The team made an exception for Willy Adames by not trading him when they felt he was integral to their culture and they did not have a replacement ready. Contreras could draw the same treatment, especially if the Brewers have some more money to play with.

William Contreras was undoubtedly the Milwaukee Brewers MVP in Game 1 of the World Series.
Contreras had an RBI single in the first inning, a walk in the sixth inning and another base hit in the eighth inning. Defensively, he caught two runners stealing to end innings and won two ABS challenges.
He became the best catcher this century to have multiple caught stealings and hits in a World Series game, per MLB Network's Sarah Langs. Joe Girardi of the New York Yankees was the last player to achieve that feat.
Girardi did it in Game 3 of the 1999 World Series against the Atlanta Braves. It had been 27 years since a catcher had a game like that, and Contreras seemed due to break the drought.
He was the best catcher in the regular season at catching runners, and the Tampa Bay Rays are a team that likes to run. Something had to give, and it was Contreras who came out on top.
At the plate, he continued a red-hot October, and the Brewers will need him to continue his hitting ways for the rest of the series. The Brewers can go up 2-0 on the Rays on Saturday, and if Contreras is swinging the bat as he has been, there is really no pitcher who is going to give him problems.
The Rays are expected to stay aggressive on the basepaths, so Contreras' arm will continue to be tested. In Game 1, he changed the complexion of the game by erasing baserunners, and could do the same in Game 2.

item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE (AP) — Trevor Megill was shouting in celebration and the Milwaukee Brewers were bolting out of the dugout to congratulate one another, believing they had just escaped a ninth-inning jam to win Game 1 of the World Series.
Not quite yet.
What initially was ruled a game-ending double play got overturned after a video review showed Brewers shortstop Cooper Pratt’s right foot was slightly off the bag when he reached to catch a high throw from second baseman Brice Turang.
No problem.
Megill regrouped and struck out Jonny DeLuca with two runners in scoring position as Milwaukee edged the Tampa Bay Rays 3-2 on Friday night.
“It’s good to get the first win out of the way,” Megill said. “That’s where all the nerves are at. First game, a lot of anticipation and build-up to where we are right now.”
The ninth inning was particularly nerve-racking for the Brewers and the sellout crowd attending Milwaukee’s first World Series game since 1982.
“You have a big range of emotions,” said team captain Christian Yelich, whose RBI triple in the first put the Brewers ahead for good. “It’s a big credit to Trev for locking back in right there and making some huge pitches after you have that emotional dump and then have to get back on it.”
Tampa Bay trailed 3-1 and hadn’t put a runner on since the sixth until it mounted its comeback attempt against Megill.
Jonathan Aranda, who went 3 for 3 with a walk, and Chandler Simpson hit consecutive one-out singles. A double steal involving pinch-runner Jorge Mateo and Simpson put runners on second and third before Junior Caminero walked on a 3-2 pitch in the dirt to load the bases.
Liam Hicks hit a grounder to the right side, and Turang ranged well to his left to field the ball before throwing to Pratt to start what initially was called a 4-6-3 double play.
Fireworks went off, players poured onto the field and Milwaukee fans roared. But then the crowd hushed as it watched the play again on the videoboard.
“You’ve got to think worst-case scenario there,” Megill said. “I thought the challenge was at first base, maybe a bobble or something. But it was pretty clear once the replay went up that it was on the play at second base. Zoomed in and it didn’t look good. It’s all right. We picked up Cooper there. He’ll pick us up tomorrow.”
The out call at second was changed to safe by umpire Alfonso Márquez at the MLB Replay Center, which caught Pratt by surprise.
“Obviously, it was close,” the 22-year-old rookie said. “I just didn’t think it was enough to overturn, so I wasn’t thinking anything of it. The video I saw, thought my cleat was dragging. … There must have been some other angles that I haven’t seen. It ultimately didn’t matter because we won.”
The Brewers won because Megill got DeLuca to swing and miss at a 2-2 pitch, capping a night in which Tampa Bay went 0 for 6 with runners in scoring position.
“This is an extremely confident group,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “You know that. We know that. They’re going to be fine. I think the frustration comes from we were one swing of the bat away right at the end of potentially taking the lead.”
The Game 1 winner has gone on to win the World Series 62.8% of the time.
This marks the first World Series featuring two teams seeking their first championship since 1980, when the Philadelphia Phillies beat the Kansas City Royals in six games. The only other major league clubs without a World Series title are the Colorado Rockies, San Diego Padres and Seattle Mariners.
Milwaukee took a 2-0 lead in the first inning against Nick Martinez. NL Cy Young Award favorite Jacob Misiorowski allowed one run and four hits over five innings to help the Brewers stay in front before relievers Abner Uribe and Aaron Ashby shut down the Rays through the eighth.
Misiorowski, who had a season-low three strikeouts, opened the game with a 103.5 mph fastball — the fastest pitch ever thrown in a World Series.
“The adrenaline kind of took over, and I tensed up and threw it hard,” said Misiorowski, who earned the win. “Then I settled down, and that was the game plan, to settle in and do me. Don’t try and overdo it.”
Milwaukee’s Jackson Chourio and William Contreras each had two hits, including an RBI single. Contreras also threw out two runners trying to steal.
Tampa Bay managed to hang around thanks in part to Martinez, who gave up those two runs in the first but held Milwaukee scoreless through the rest of his five-inning stint. The Brewers added an insurance run in the seventh when Chourio singled home Pratt.
Then came all the action in the ninth, with the Brewers’ premature celebration followed by a team-wide sigh of relief as Pratt offered some parting words to Megill.
“I just said, ‘Thank you, man. Thanks for picking me up,’” Pratt said. “That’s what this game is. It’s a game of pick-me-up. He picked me up today.”
Up next
Drew Rasmussen (16-5, 2.67 ERA) pitches for Tampa Bay and Logan Henderson (11-3, 2.47) starts for Milwaukee in Game 2 on Saturday night. In this postseason, Rasmussen is 2-0 with a 1.29 ERA and Henderson is 0-0 with a 3.00 ERA.

Brewers' Jacob Misiorowski drops brutally honest admission on his Game 1 start appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Milwaukee Brewers possessed a top-notch bullpen in the regular season and in the last two rounds of the playoffs, but the idea of this team winning a championship without Jacob Misiorowski posting his best stuff seemed near-incomprehensible. The presumptive National League Cy Young was unable to reach the sixth inning for a third straight postseason start, and yet, the Brew Crew are now just three wins away from capturing their first World Series title in franchise history.
Misiorowski pitched five innings of one-run ball in Friday's 3-2 Game 1 victory versus the Tampa Bay Rays, allowing four hits while recording three strikeouts and one walk. He perfectly described his fairly short yet triumphant outing.
"Not perfect, good enough to get a win," the genial 24-year-old right-hander said, via Joey Mistretta of ClutchPoints.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Misiorowski has not been operating as a work horse for some time. He has accumulated only a combined 13 1/3 innings of work across three playoff outings. The three Ks are also surprisingly low. This record-breaking flamethrower is nearing the end of his first full MLB campaign, and he is showing the effects of unleashing elite velocity all yearlong.
Like Misiorowski said, though, he had enough on this night. The Brewers' bullpen also provided first-class reinforcements, once again. Aaron Ashby remains unstoppable, Abner Uribe enjoyed a stellar showing in his own right and Trevor Megill survived despite allowing one run in the ninth. The lineup notched timely hits, as it does, and All-Star catcher William Contreras threw out potential game-tying runs multiple times.
Jacob Misiorowski did not carry the squad to a 1-0 series lead in American Family Field. Pat Murphy has not asked him to fill that role during this postseason. Milwaukee secured the W by putting forth a complete effort. This ballclub may not have many household names, but it should be obvious by now that one player does not define Brewers baseball.
If Milwaukee has its way, Misiorowski will not have to put the team on his back again for the rest of 2026. Game 2 is Saturday at approximately 8 p.m. ET.

If you expected the Milwaukee Brewers to enter the World Series without making any adjustments, you must not have been watching the team this season. Even after sweeping the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS and overcoming a red-hot Padres squad in the Division Series, manager Pat Murphy is always finding new ways to keep his opponents on their toes.
The Brewers released their batting order on Friday afternoon, just hours before first pitch. Their updated order will be as follows:
1. Jackson Chourio
2. Jake Bauers
3. Christian Yelich
4. William Contreras
5. Brice Turang
6. Garrett Mitchell
7. Cooper Pratt
8. Sal Frelick
9. David Hamilton
What should we take away from the Milwaukee Brewers' updated batting order for Game 1 of the World Series?
This new-look order should give the Brewers an interesting dynamic of staggering lefty and righty batters, likely in hopes of keeping Game 1 starter Nick Martinez, a righty, out of a consistent rhythm to begin the contest. By moving Contreras to fourth, it sets up Milwaukee's best home run hitter this postseason for a grand slam opportunity, should it arise. Meanwhile, Yelich at the third spot gives the Brew Crew a likely opportunity for some much-needed contact hitting early in the rotation.
It's far from surprising to see first baseman Jake Bauers taking such a firm position near the top of the batting order, as Bauers emerged as one of the most reliable offensive threats on the team, and frankly, in all of baseball. His ability to extend the pitch count and make contact persistently has been a thorn in the sides of pitchers everywhere, so this is likely Murphy's best attempt to extend Martinez's pitch count early.
Meanwhile, Turang slotting back into the fifth spot in the lineup makes sense given his inconsistent production thus far in the postseason. Through eight games, the 26-year-old is hitting just .222 with six hits to seven strikeouts. The good news, however, is that Turang turned a corner in the Dodgers series, logging hits in three of four hits, while scoring a run in each contest.
The end of the lineup should be of interest as well. All year long, Brewers fans grappled with questions over David Hamilton's place in the lineup, but through the postseason, he's certainly proving he belongs. Milwaukee is in serious need of some production late in the order, so all eyes will be on Hamilton, as well as Cooper Pratt and Sal Frelick, to carry that torch.
Overall, this is a wise move by Pat Murphy to make sure his lineup isn't identical to what Tampa Bay was expecting to see. Although the players are the same, a little shake-up in the order might force Martinez and the Rays' defense to think twice, which is all the Brewers can really ask for in a matchup of two teams that are this talented defensively.

The Brewers, whose 103 regular-season wins were a franchise record, navigated a tight NL Division Series against the Padres before clobbering the two-time reigning champion Dodgers in the NL Championship Series sweep. It’s just the second World Series appearance in their history and their first since 1982.
Meanwhile, the Rays swept the division rival Yankees in the ALDS before handling the Guardians in six games in the ALCS. They’re back in the Fall Classic for the third time and the first since 2020.
Both teams do a little bit of everything right on the diamond, making for what should be a thoroughly exciting World Series. Here’s how our group of MLB.com experts see it playing out.
Rays vs. Brewers
The pick: Brewers (43 of 51 votes, 84.3%)
Why they’ll win
Any time you take down the back-to-back reigning champs, and do so in a sweep, it’s going to make noise. But really, this is nothing new for the 2026 Brewers. They owned the best regular-season record with a roster that just gets the job done across the board.
The Brewers can play small ball, but they can slug when it matters most, too. In fact, Milwaukee has been more homer-dependent in October than it was all year. But the club can still work a deep count and get on base in many ways. Just ask Jake Bauers.
On the mound, it’s no secret that the bullpen is the Brewers’ strength. One of the best groups in the regular season is only doing more of the same in October, with a 1.33 ERA in eight games. Lefty Aaron Ashby is leading the charge during a historically good run. And then there’s that Jacob Misiorowski guy, who has been good enough in the playoffs but could unleash a new, dominant level in the World Series.
What they’re saying
“There's something about this Brewers club. Maintaining the league's best record all summer and barely giving an inch so far in the postseason, they're looking pretty unstoppable with the right mix of clutch hits, key performers and an absolutely lockdown bullpen. It might finally be the Crew's moment in the spotlight.” -- Adrian Garro, editorial producer
“The Brewers have been knocking on this door for years and are firing on all cylinders following their impressive sweep of the Dodgers. They are smart and hard-nosed enough not to let the long layoff affect them negatively.” -- Andrew Werle, supervising editor, content operations
“Walking off Mason Miller. Sweeping the 2-time defending champion Dodgers. These Brewers may just be a team of destiny, with their final obstacle being the American League's top-seeded Rays.” -- Kyle Boris, supervisor, media operations
The dissenting view
The Brewers have been dominant, but so have the Rays. They have a clear edge in starting pitching, with Drew Rasmussen, Freddy Peralta and Nick Martinez firing on all cylinders. The Tampa Bay bullpen, while not as overpowering as the Brewers’, is still strong and has lockdown closer Bryan Baker waiting in the wings.
The key for the Rays likely lies in their lineup, where Junior Caminero, Yandy Díaz and Jonathan Aranda appear to be heating up at the right time. Much like Milwaukee, the Rays will put together quality at-bats, get on base and then cause havoc on the basepaths. Perhaps no one is more adept at doing so than Chandler Simpson.
“The Rays' ‘small ball’ doesn't slump, and they've been pressing all of the right pitching buttons.” -- Jonathan Mayo, national reporter, prospects
“With their Big 3 of Yandy Díaz, Jonathan Aranda and Junior Caminero breaking out at the end of the ALCS -- plus a slight edge over the Crew in starting pitching -- I believe the Rays are going to steal Game 1 vs. The Miz and ride that to a World Series title. Third time is a charm.” -- Brian McGrath, supervising editor, content operations

It’s not hard to see why Chourio was our experts’ favorite to take home the World Series Most Valuable Player Award. Still just 22 years old, Chourio already leads Brewers franchise history with six career playoff home runs. He’s already shown he can rise to the occasion this year with a walk-off single against Mason Miller in the NLDS and a massive homer against Blake Snell in the NLCS. But Chourio’s overall production this October has been quiet (6-for-35). It might just be a matter of time before he breaks out.
“Chourio is due to break out in the World Series. While he hasn't done much in the playoffs so far, his two homers were impactful -- a go-ahead shot and a game-tying blast. He's ready to let it rip.” -- Kelsie Heneghan, senior coordinator, social media editorial, MiLB
“He's a legend in the making. This is the start of his Hall of Fame case.” -- Will Leitch, senior columnist

Megill has been lights-out as the Brewers’ closer, so it’s easy to envision him shutting things down at American Family Field in Game 6 or 7. But don’t be surprised if it’s Ashby continuing his fireman role -- or The Miz coming in for a clutch relief appearance.

item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE (AP) — The Miz will try to whiz his famous fastball by batters on baseball's biggest stage, opening a new-look World Series between teams guaranteed to produce a first-time champion.
Jacob Misiorowski brings his record-setting heat to the mound for the Milwaukee Brewers on Friday night when he throws the first pitch of the best-of-seven championship against the Tampa Bay Rays, a matchup of modest-money marvels who bumped off glamorous rivals with a throwback base-to-base style.
“Forrest Gump, everyone,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said Thursday, introducing his ace to the assembled media.
“I'm still fresh to all of this and I have no idea what the hell is going on,” Misiorowski said a few minutes later.
Few predicted this pairing of pennant winners when the season opened March 25. The first World Series with robot umpires is the first since 1980 between teams seeking their first championship and also could be the first with a 104 mph pitch — thanks to Misiorowski — and the first to be played totally indoors.
Milwaukee is in the Series for the second time after a 44-year absence — an appropriate number given that it was the jersey of the Cream City's most famous baseball player, Hank Aaron, who became a star with the Milwaukee Braves in the 1950s and ended his career with the expansion Brewers in the 1970s.
Both teams fell short in previous Series trips, the Brewers losing to St. Louis in 1982 and the Rays to Philadelphia in 2008 and to the Los Angeles Dodgers in 2020. Not since the Phillies beat Kansas City in 1980 have two teams met seeking their first title. The time before that was in 1920.
Rays players are excited to display their brand of baseball.
“We love watching those guys cause chaos,” Tampa Bay pitcher Steven Matz said of his team's bunters and speedsters. “Every time it’s first and third and someone lays down a bunt, we are just dying laughing in the bullpen.”
Misiorowski is likely to set a World Series velocity record
Misiorowski, a 24-year-old right-hander in his first full major league season, is a starting pitcher like no other. He threw 1,115 pitches of 100 mph or higher this year — shattering the old high of 673 since tracking began in 2008, by Jordan Hicks in 2018.
His fastest pitch was 105.5 mph to the Chicago Cubs' Pete Crow-Armstrong on June 27, and he appears likely to break the 101.1 mph record for a Series starter by the New York Mets' Noah Syndergaard in 2015 and possibly the overall Series high of 103.2 mph by Cubs reliever Aroldis Chapman to Cleveland's Coco Crisp in Game 2 of 2016.
Misiorowski didn't finish the fifth inning in either of his first two postseason starts this year. Batters have swung at 94 of his 182 postseason pitches and fouled off 51 — 28% of pitches and 54% of swings.
“He hasn’t been as crisp,” Murphy said. “They’re obviously looking at an area. They’re trying to exploit everything. He’s exposed, like all these guys get at some point.”
Martinez a surprise starter for Rays
Nick Martinez will start for Tampa Bay, which gives extra rest to Drew Rasmussen ahead of Game 2 and Freddy Peralta before Game 3.
A 36-year-old right-hander with his fourth major league team, Martinez took the Rays to dinner Wednesday at Carnevor, a top Milwaukee steakhouse. He invites teammates, who have nicknamed him “El Presidente,” to a restaurant in every road city.
“To when I first got to the league, I’ve been around guys that knew how to control a clubhouse and for lack of a better term, knew how to throw a party,” Martinez said. “Getting the guys together is important. Creating that off-the-field chemistry translates to on the field.”
Brewers and Rays have throwback offenses
In an age where power bats usually rule, Milwaukee scored a major league-low 32.1% of its runs on homers and Tampa Bay was second-lowest at 34.4%, according to the Elias Sports Bureau.
Brewers captain Christian Yelich says “we’ve done a good job of being kind of chameleons.”
“It's cool that you don't have to be the team to hit 170 home runs a game or whatever,” Misiorowski said. “You can win a baseball game so many different ways.”
Rays batters had the fewest strikeouts among the 30 teams and Tampa Bay’s 45 sacrifice bunts were the most among American League teams since 2015.
“If we had a club that was built with a bunch of boppers, we probably wouldn’t be bunting and stealing bases,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “I think we already have made bunting cool.”
After back-to-back Dodgers titles, MLB will have a small-payroll champion
This marks the first time since 1991 that both Series teams are in the bottom half of payrolls: the Brewers were 19th as of Aug. 31 and the Rays 25th. Milwaukee, MLB's smallest market, could become the first small-market champion since Kansas City in 2015. The Rays rank 15th in market size.
To reach the Series, the Brewers swept the deep-pocketed, two-time champion Dodgers in the NL Championship Series and the Rays swept the New York Yankees in an AL Division Series.
Yelich, the highest-paid player in the Series, was 44th overall in the majors on opening day. Yandy Díaz, who earns most among the Rays, ranked 154th.
Robot umps are changing games
Batters have succeeded on 63% of challenges during the postseason in the first year of the Automated Ball-Strike System, winning 40 of 63 appeals to the robot umps. That is up from 49% during the regular season.
Catchers' 58% success rate in the playoffs (58 of 99) is down a tick from 59% during the regular season and pitchers are 1 for 1 — Tampa Bay’s Griffin Jax made the only challenge. The 60% overall rate is up from 54% in the regular season.
Tampa Bay's batters have yet to make a postseason challenge. Milwaukee's have won 4 of 7, including a perfect 2 for 2 by Jake Bauers.
Brewers catcher William Contreras has won 60% (12 of 20) and Rays catcher Liam Hicks 67% (8 of 12).
Rest vs. rust: Extra time off hasn't been helpful in recent years
Milwaukee will have had seven days off going into the opener.
While teams with less rest are 15-15 in the Series since Wild Card Era started in 1995, they are 12-4 since 2009.
___
Ronald Blum, The Associated Press

(Photo credit: Benny Sieu)
MILWAUKEE -- The Milwaukee Brewers will be looking for hard-throwing Jacob Misiorowski to regain his dominant regular-season form against the visiting Tampa Bay Rays on Friday in the opening game of the World Series.
Misiorowski, who often tops 100 mph with his fastball, will be opposed by veteran right-hander Nick Martinez in a matchup of teams that have not won the World Series. It is the first meeting of two teams without a World Series title since the Philadelphia Phillies topped the Kansas City Royals in six games in 1980.
Milwaukee, which won a franchise-record 103 games during the regular season, advanced with a four-game sweep of the two-time defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series, while the Rays ousted the Cleveland Guardians in six games in the American League Championship Series.
The Brewers' only other World Series appearance was in 1982 when they were in the American League. The charismatic 'Harvey's Wallbangers' lost 6-3 to the St. Louis Cardinals in the decisive seventh game.
The Rays will be making their third World Series appearance. They lost to Philadelphia in five games in 2008 and in six games to the Dodgers in 2020.
Misiorowski, considered the favorite for the NL Cy Young Award, was 16-5 with a 1.80 ERA and 252 strikeouts. The latter two stats were best in the majors.
But the 24-year-old right-hander did not make it through five innings in either postseason start, although the Brewers rallied to win both games. They topped the San Diego Padres 3-2 in Game 1 of the National League Division Series and the Dodgers 2-1 in the NLCS opener.
'I feel good. I feel like the first one might have been a little under what I expected, but the second one was pretty much right where I wanted to be,' Misiorowski said.
Misiorowski worked out of trouble in his postseason starts, allowing three runs on nine hits in 8 1/3 innings with 11 strikeouts and four walks.
'He hasn't been as crisp,' Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy said. 'I don't think people are up there thinking it's going to be 104 (mph), and I think they're elated if it's anything less than that. They're obviously looking at an area. They're trying to exploit everything. He's exposed, like all these guys get at some point.'
At the back end, the Brewers' bullpen has allowed six runs over 40 2/3 innings for a 1.33 ERA in the postseason. Closer Trevor Megill has four saves after collecting 30 in the regular season.
Milwaukee was last in the NL in home runs (154) during the regular season but leads all teams in the postseason with 10 homers in eight games. The Rays have hit seven in nine games.
Catcher William Contreras batted .367 with three homers and five RBIs over the Brewers' first two series. Outfielder Jackson Chourio hit .171, but he had two homers and a team-high seven RBIs.
Jake Bauers, who reached the majors with the Rays in 2018, was named the NLCS Most Valuable Player after hitting .286 with one homer and six RBIs against the Dodgers. Bauers set career highs with 26 homers and 86 RBIs during the regular season.
The 36-year-old Martinez pitched in the postseason with San Diego in 2022 and the Cincinnati Reds last season, but he will be making his World Series debut Friday. Ace Drew Rasmussen will start Game 2 with an extra day's rest, with former Brewers ace Freddy Peralta to follow in Game 3.
'It's exciting,' Martinez said Thursday. 'I think as a team, as a staff, we're confident in whoever we call up for the mound. It fell on me, and my job is just to rack up as many outs as we can and keep us in this ballgame.'
Martinez picked up the win in Game 4 of the ALCS when the Rays evened the series with a 7-3 victory at Cleveland. He allowed one run on two hits in 5 1/3 innings.
'He was pitching in pretty cold weather in Cleveland,' said Rays manager Kevin Cash, who was also at the helm for the 2020 World Series. 'Made some adjustments, he got the strike throwing where he wanted, the cutter gone, and the changeup. I don't even know, somebody told me he changed his grip in between innings, between the first and second. I'm glad I didn't know that in the moment.'
Martinez also started Game 3 in the Rays' ALDS sweep of the New York Yankees. He gave up two runs in 3 2/3 innings in an eventual 4-3 Tampa Bay victory.
Martinez is 0-1 with a 4.44 ERA in 12 regular-season games (seven starts) against Milwaukee. He has a 2.93 ERA in eight games at American Family Field.
Rays closer Bryan Baker, who tied for the MLB lead with 41 saves, has five saves in five postseason chances, pitching in seven of the nine games.
Third baseman Junior Caminero, whose 42 homers were second in the AL, has just one hit in 33 at-bats in the postseason.
--Jim Hoehn, Field Level Media

Welcome to a most fantastically interesting World Series, in which focusing on the size of the markets involved completely misses the forest for the trees. It’s a No. 1-vs.-No. 1 matchup, just the sixth time in the past 30 years that’s happened. It’s a pair of fanbases who have never won before, which marks the first time since 1980 (Royals vs. Phillies) that’s happened, and thus only the second time in more than a century, since the previous time had been 1920.
It’s a matchup of teams that have more than a few connections. Note that Tampa Bay’s top two starters, Drew Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta, each came up with Milwaukee, and were teammates on the 2020-21 Brewers. Note, also, that NLCS MVP Jake Bauers made his debut with Tampa Bay back in 2018, and that Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold spent nine years in the Tampa Bay front office before moving to Wisconsin.
It's more than just that. Depending on how you view your baseball aesthetics, it's a delightfully throwback sort of on-field style. It’s not that these teams eschew analytical thinking -- exactly the opposite, really -- but no team struck out less than the Rays, each team finished in the top five in steals and the bottom 10 in homers, and the bunt hits leaderboard goes “Tampa Bay first, Milwaukee second.”
Throw in a pair of excellent defenses, and you know what you’re going to get here, which is excellent baseball played by a pair of teams that actually look a whole lot like one another. We know what else we're going to get, too: an incredibly interesting series. Which side has the edge?
Catcher
William Contreras, over the past five years, has a pretty solid argument to make as being the best all-around catcher in the National League. While his bat over the last two seasons (110 OPS+) isn’t quite what it was at his peak from 2022-24 (129 OPS+), it’s reliably solid, and then of course he’s been fantastic in eight playoff games, posting a 1.157 OPS with three homers. It’s hard to overstate how important the midseason acquisition of Liam Hicks (129 OPS+ in 41 games for Tampa Bay) was, really helping to lengthen a top-heavy lineup, though he hasn’t done much with the bat in the playoffs. Given relatively similar defensive value, we’ll give a small edge based on track record.
Advantage: Brewers
First base
It's a tale of two winding paths here, as Jonathan Aranda finally had his breakout last season, a decade after he signed as an amateur free agent with Tampa Bay, and of course Jake Bauers' long road to get to this point has been well-chronicled. Bauers has the offensive edge both in terms of power and getting on base, and neither are terribly strong defensive players, so given the mild 2026 regular-season advantage and also the superior performance in October, it’s hard not to choose Bauers on this. Great stories, both.
Advantage: Brewers
Second base
Brice Turang is the best all-around second baseman in the game, pairing excellent defense with a more recently found power stroke, popping 21 homers and driving in 100. The Rays have certainly found some ways to get value out of their second-base duo of Richie Palacios and Ben Williamson, but it’s a relatively below-average spot for Tampa Bay and, either way, we’re comparing to Milwaukee’s best-in-class superstar. This one is probably the biggest mismatch of any pairing on the list.
Advantage: Brewers
Shortstop
Here’s how you know how well-regarded Taylor Walls is on defense: The Rays continue to play him every day despite a near-total lack of offense from the position, as he’s posted all of a .381 OPS this month, and even that was juiced a little by the inexplicable three walks that Cleveland issued him in ALCS Game 6. It’s not just a small-sample thing, either, as Walls has been a routinely ineffective hitter for the entirety of his career.
There’s no doubt that Milwaukee’s Cooper Pratt is a stronger offensive force, though that’s been more good than great, with a league-average line as a rookie and a mostly singles-based approach in the playoffs. While he’s expected to be a quality shortstop as his career progresses, a number of important miscues in the postseason tilt this one to the more surehanded Walls.
Advantage: Rays
Third base
If there’s some argument that this series features more depth than true superstars, then that case falls apart a little at third, where Tampa Bay’s Junior Caminero posted his second consecutive 40-plus homer season on his way to, most likely, some high placement on AL MVP ballots. It’s true that prior to his ALCS Game 6 homer, his bat had been relatively quiet in October, but we’re also talking about all of eight games against some of the best pitching the sport has to offer. (The average fastball he’s seen? 96.8 mph.) There’s an obvious speed-and-defense edge for Milwaukee in David Hamilton and Joey Ortiz, but not quite so much that you’d take either or both over Caminero, or that it’s really close at all.
Advantage: Rays
Left field
This is actually the most fun comparison, because who do you like more, the 22-year-old power-and-defense superstar in Jackson Chourio -- the only player in history to have three 20-20 seasons through age-22 -- or the 25-year-old elite speed-and-contact guy in Chandler Simpson, who improved his defense to the point that both were named Gold Glove finalists last week? It’s yet another reminder that there’s more than one way to provide value, and certainly both teams are very pleased with their situations here. It’s hard, though, not to default to Chourio, who might already be a top-20 position player in the sport. If both can run and field, and only one has any power, then the advantage writes itself.
Advantage: Brewers
Center field
In Garrett Mitchell and Jonny DeLuca, you have two very strong defensive center fielders, though you’d probably give the slight edge here to DeLuca. (Cedric Mullins also carries a good glove, though this spot has belonged to DeLuca all month.) The question about their bats is what shape of production you prefer, in that Mitchell struck out considerably more than DeLuca, but he also had an on-base percentage 54 points higher, thanks in large part to a walk rate three times as high. While we’re not weighing postseason performance too much here, it’s worth noting that Mitchell has had some huge hits, while DeLuca mostly has not. This is about as razor-thin as we’ll see here, but even if Mitchell’s glove isn’t as good, it’s still good, and he gets on base. Edge, Milwaukee. A small one, anyway.
Advantage: Brewers
Right field
For everything that Sal Frelick has done for the Brewers over his four seasons with the team -- and he has done quite a bit -- this was not a terribly strong season for him, posting a career-worst 70 OPS+, and he’s managed only three singles and a few walks in the playoffs. That’s not to say that he can’t help the team win in other ways, because he can and does, but Tampa Bay’s Victor Mesa Jr. has been one of the team’s breakout stars, putting up not only a 127 OPS+ but also some truly elite defensive metrics, in just half a season. You’re already familiar, anyway, with his absolute cannon of a throwing arm. Mesa Jr. wasn’t on the Opening Day roster and didn’t even join the Rays for good until late May. He might just be one of the most important players in the World Series, though.
Advantage: Rays
Designated hitter
It would be hard to find two players who mean more to their respective teams than veterans Yandy Díaz (in his eighth season with Tampa Bay) and recently appointed Milwaukee captain Christian Yelich (in his ninth season as a Brewer). Neither plays the field much anymore, nor is either at or near their peak of offensive performance these days. But Díaz far outperformed Yelich during the regular season (124 OPS+ to 91 OPS+, where again, 100 is average), and that’s held true in the postseason, too, where Yelich has been held out of certain games against tough lefties in favor of Andrew Vaughn. At DH, literally the only thing that matters is “dangerous bat,” and that’s Díaz still, after all these years.
Advantage: Rays
Starting pitchers
If we’re talking about each team’s top three starters, which represent the bulk of a postseason rotation, then it’s Jacob Misiorowski, Logan Henderson and Robert Gasser for Milwaukee, and Drew Rasmussen, Freddy Peralta and Nick Martinez for Tampa Bay. Those six pitchers, so far in the playoffs, have combined for a 1.87 ERA. They’re not that good, obviously, with every underlying metric saying that the strikeout rate has been just average, and that they’ve been bailed out to some extent by excellent defense and relief pitching.
Still: When Misiorowski -- the presumptive NL Cy Young winner, the most dominant per-batter pitcher of the moment -- has the highest postseason ERA of these six, you know how strong each team is here. You really can’t look at full-season stats, either, because it goes without saying that the Tampa Bay version of Peralta is a very different pitcher than New York version we saw prior to the Trade Deadline. Misiorowski is the best of the six, but is he that much better than Rasmussen right now, himself an ace? Maybe not.
These are two strengths, but we like Tampa Bay ever so slightly more for one reason: depth. No Milwaukee starter, not even the top ones, has managed to get past five innings in the playoffs so far, which puts a lot of pressure on the bullpens. (There’s a particularly interesting angle here if Tampa Bay’s high-contact, flat-swing hitters can foul off enough Misiorowski pitches to wear him out, as has already happened to him this month.) If you look past the top three, you’d probably take Tampa Bay’s Griffin Jax and Ian Seymour to get outs a little more than Milwaukee’s Shane Drohan and Dustin May.
They’re both good, obviously. They’re World Series starting rotations. We’d give the ever-so-slight edge to Tampa Bay in a best of seven.
Advantage: Rays
Relief pitchers
If Milwaukee’s starters have been more good than great this month, then their relievers have more than picked up the slack, as you’ve almost certainly heard the note that in 40 2/3 postseason innings, the Brewers' bullpen has allowed all of six earned runs. While most of the focus there lands on Aaron Ashby or closer Trevor Megill, realize that JoJo Romero has a 47% strikeout rate this month, and that Abner Uribe, Antonio Senzatela, Megill and Ashby are all averaging more than 98 mph on their heaters this month. In fact, it is the second-hardest-throwing bullpen of the pitch tracking era (since 2008) -- at 98 mph even -- and the hardest that doesn’t include Mason Miller.
It makes, then, for an ironic matchup against a Tampa Bay bullpen that is A) also very good but B) does not throw hard, comparatively, at just 93.2 mph. (That goes down slightly, if you don't include Peralta’s impressive appearance in ALCS Game 4.) Much depends on the status of Bryan Baker, their All-Star closer, who was used so heavily against Cleveland that his fastball, which averaged 96.3 mph during the regular season, sunk below 93 mph in ALCS Game 6.
He was still good, of course. All the Rays are. It’s just hard not to go with Milwaukee, given their superior depth and full rest.
Advantage: Brewers
Prediction
It should be clear by now that this is an incredibly tightly matched series between two mirror-image teams, the best in their respective leagues, and you could as easily claim “rust or rest” for Milwaukee after their layoff, no matter which narrative you’d like to go with. Milwaukee has the biggest-name pitcher in Misiorowski; Tampa Bay has clearly the biggest star hitter in Caminero; and both sides play strong defense and win in ways that aren’t just waiting for the homer.
We like that Milwaukee has the home-field advantage, and the bullpen edge, and also that their lineup just seems a little deeper; in the second half of the season, no team -- not the Dodgers, not the Cubs, not anyone -- got more production from the No. 6 through 9 spots in their lineup than Milwaukee. That’s in part because of the middle infield, where the Brewers were third best, while Tampa Bay was third weakest. There’s at least some question about what shape Baker will be in, though three days of rest before the World Series ought to help.
It won’t be a cakewalk, because there’s too much talent and similarity on both sides for that. But every small edge matters, and Milwaukee has enough of them that we expect the second World Series title in city history, and the first for the Brewers franchise. Get ready to slide, Bernie.
Brewers in seven.

The Milwaukee Brewers' World Series roster should look almost exactly the same as it has so far this postseason.
Fresh off a dominant sweep in the NLCS against the back-to-back World Series champion Dodgers, the Brewers had a full week to prepare for this winner-take-all best-of-seven series.
Looking at the Rays lineup and how they construct things, it'll be interesting to see what Murphy goes with in the upcoming series.
Remember, Milwaukee has a pair of pitchers who have yet to pitch in the postseason despite being on the roster the entire time.
If there was ever a time for Big Woo to come back, it would be now, though the team must carefully weigh all of its options before pulling the trigger.
Infielders:
- Jake Bauers
- David Hamilton
- Joey Ortiz
- Cooper Pratt
- Brice Turang
- Andrew Vaughn
Outfielders
- Jackson Chourio
- Sal Frelick
- Luis Lara
- Garrett Mitchell
- Christian Yelich
Catchers
- William Contreras
- Gary Sanchez
Pitchers
- Aaron Ashby
- Shane Drohan
- Robert Gasser

- Dustin May

- Jacob Misiorowski
- Chad Patrick
- JoJo Romero
- Antonio Senzatela
- Abner Uribe
- Brandon Woodruff
Brewers make one roster change
When it comes to William Contreras and Gary Sanchez, neither of those players is going anywhere. Sanchez has yet to catch in the playoffs, and he likely won't, but he had a huge pinch-hit walk against Mason Miller in Game 2 of the NLDS.
Milwaukee will still carry six infielders and five outfielders. There isn't a world where they should mess with any of those 11 players. There are no injuries that have been made available to the public, and there's no one else who could fill those spots at this point in the year.
Pitching-wise, Chad Patrick has gotten loose a few times, so that's the only thing keeping him on the roster.
Woodruff shouldn't start a game unless it's at home and he's used as an opener. But, with where he's at, it certainly feels like he could give this team some useful bullpen innings, and there's no one more deserving to be on the roster than him.

(Translated from Spanish)
Let me tell you something about baseball: No one knows f***ing anything.
Every year, it’s the spring, you hear people talk. “The Brewers, I’m thinking they got lucky to win all those games last year … until the end, and then their luck ran out. They went as far as they can go.” OK!!! I mean, I just have to laugh. The playoff series against the Dodgers, we got swept…… It was terrible. I understand why there was not so much belief in us after a loss like that. But if you want the truth, I’ll tell you, because I was there. I’m the one who saw it from both sides, right? I’m behind the plate for their side … and I’m at the plate for our side. Here’s the truth: The Dodgers were the lucky team last season.
No, I’m not saying they were lucky to be champions. Of course not. It’s a tremendous team, with tremendous players. I’ll take nothing away from them. But were they lucky to SWEEP us? That’s a different story. Between their team and our team, 4–0, that wasn’t the gap. But they made the plays, got the breaks, and by the end of the series we were in our own heads. We’re thinking, Those guys…….. they found the magic. How else do you explain it??? You can’t. After the series, though, a lot of people thought they could explain it. They were like, “That’s how it will always go when those teams play….. The Brewers will lose. It’s too many stars, too many Hall of Famers, too many great players.” People thought that four games told the whole story. And the story to them, it’s how we weren’t good enough. How we couldn’t win the World Series with this group.
But anyone who thinks that way....... to be honest, they don’t know baseball. OF COURSE we could win the World Series with this group!!! Come on. Just look at our wins since I’ve been here: 92, 93, 97, 103. To me, that says a lot about who we are. We’re always on top of our division, and always improving. And maybe that’s not exciting to some people … but it’s our sport. Grinding and making these little adjustments. Maybe you focus on a few things over the winter. Maybe you sign a few new guys. Maybe a few young guys step up. Maybe you grow a little mentally tougher, a little hungrier. And then you train in the spring, and then you see what you got in the summer, and then you try to capture some magic in the fall. And if it doesn’t go your way, then you get back to work in the winter and you do the thing over again. So I’m hearing people bury us after getting swept last season and I’m like, What??? That was four games. That’s a short story.
Baseball, it’s a LONG story.
Just ask Pat. He’s in the game all his life, it’s 65 years until someone gives him a chance to be the man!!! Then he gets his chance and now my guy is the best manager in the league. Or just ask Christian. He’s an MVP ... then he deals with these injuries, it’s so tough. But nothing tougher than HIM, he sets the standard and that’s our captain. Or just ask Jake. Dude is almost gonna retire…… wow. Then he comes back, to help his family out, and now he’s letting it rip. Or just ask Brewers fans. The most unbelievable fans. They’re so loyal. But a lot of them never seen a World Series game in Milwaukee!!! And they never won it all. It’s crazy. Or honestly, man...... even just ask me. 15 years ago? I’m a kid in Puerto Cabello, trying to catch the eyes of some scouts. 10 years ago? I’m a teenager in rookie ball, watching my big bro win his ring with the Cubs. 5 years ago? I’m a backup catcher in Atlanta, working to earn those big league at-bats. And now I’m here.
So it’s almost like, to get to THIS moment, we had to have those other moments. Had to take the long way, I swear. And I think the team we are now, how we play fearless, that’s where it comes from. We fear nothing, because we’ve experienced everything. When we got swept like that….. it’s disappointment, heartbreak, embarrassment, all those things. So then a year later, Brewers / Dodgers AGAIN, we win the first three but they go up 4–0 in Game 4 … of course we know what everyone’s thinking. About to be Red Sox / Yankees 2004. Dodgers won four in a row last year, they’ll do it again. OK. But what are WE thinking? What’s the vibe in OUR dugout? I actually won’t even say it was calm. It wasn’t calm! It was more, Nahhhhh..... LET’S END THIS. So that’s what we did.
And just like last year when they swept us, and I said they were lucky to do that, I know this year we were probably lucky to sweep them. I won’t sit here and tell you the Brewers are unstoppable. I’ve been around. I know how quickly things can change in this game. Being hot in your last series, it doesn’t mean you stay hot in your next one. But I’ll tell you this: We’re a great team. We’ve been a great team. It’s just that every year, we’ve run into a team where it’s like, Those guys……. they found the magic. Now it’s THE WORLD SERIES though — so I guess it’s only two options left??? Either we’re about to run into them, or we are them.
–William

The 2026 World Series is going to make history. Either the Tampa Bay Rays or Milwaukee Brewers are about to claim their first championship.
So, that's what's at stake. But what should everyone expect?
According to FanDuel, the Brewers are the favorite (-172) and the Rays are the underdog (+148). Yet this is ultimately a 103-win team against a 98-win team, and both clubs play a very similar style of baseball.
It's therefore worth getting in depth with the specifics of this matchup before making any predictions. Who are the key players? What are the key matchups? What are the X-factors that will determine the series?
Let's see what we can see, and then we'll present picks for the winner of the World Series and for the World Series MVP.
World Series Schedule
1 of 6
All Games on Fox
Game 1 (Friday, October 23): Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 2 (Saturday, October 24): Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 3 (Monday, October 26): Milwaukee at Tampa Bay, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 4 (Tuesday, October 27): Milwaukee at Tampa Bay, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 5 (Wednesday, October 28)*: Milwaukee at Tampa Bay, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 6 (Friday, October 30)*: Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8:00 p.m. ET
Game 7 (Saturday, October 31)*: Tampa Bay at Milwaukee, 8:00 p.m. ET
*If necessary
Key Players for the Rays
2 of 6
3B Junior Caminero
Caminero has been the driving force in the Rays' lineup over the last two seasons, slamming over 40 home runs and racking up over 100 RBI in each. Yet he went cool with a season-low .772 OPS in September, and he initially struggled to snap out of it once the postseason began.
That changed in the last three games of the ALCS. The 23-year-old had hits in all three, including a home run in the clincher that he soaked in as much as possible (and then some). Is he back? It sure seems like he's back.
DH Yandy Díaz
Even if he's not as big of a power threat as Caminero, Díaz rarely fails to have a good at-bat or to hit the ball on a line. He's hit an even .300 across the last four seasons, and he led the AL in hits this year.
The 35-year-old was not the MVP of the ALCS, but he could have been. He torched the Cleveland Guardians for a 1.061 OPS and six extra-base hits, culminating in the two-run homer that iced Game 6.
RHP Drew Rasmussen
Even if he didn't get a ton of hype, Rasmussen was a ball-knower's ace in the regular season between 2022 and 2026. He posted a sub-3.00 ERA annually, and he even led the AL in WHIP this season.
Now the secret is out. The 31-year-old's three starts in the playoffs have yielded just three earned runs in 21.0 innings, with 23 strikeouts and only three walks. His changeup has been especially lethal, holding hitters to three hits in 24 at-bats.
RHP Freddy Peralta
Peralta was with the Brewers this time last year, and his journey since then has taken him to lows with the New York Mets and now highs again with the Rays. He's coming into the World Series hot off being named the ALCS MVP.
The 30-year-old doesn't offer a complicated scouting report. He's throwing his fastball about 70 percent of the time in October, daring hitters to beat him on his best pitch. They haven't, going just 8-for-39 against it so far.
RHP Bryan Baker
Baker blew his third save of the year back on May 13. He hasn't blown one since in 53 turns on the mound, along the way allowing just five earned runs in 52.0 innings.
The 31-year-old's velocity has declined throughout the year, but that has yet to translate into any kind of advantage for hitters. It could be because he uses his fastball and changeup in roughly equal tandem, using both to hold hitters to one hit in 21 at-bats thus far in October.
Key Players for the Brewers
3 of 6
LF Jackson Chourio
The Brewers signed Chourio to an $84 million contract before he had played even one game in the majors. It has paid off in the form of three straight 20-20 seasons, and all before he's turned even 23 years old.
On paper, his .171 batting average and .553 OPS say he's not having a good postseason. Yet even if the Brewers would like more consistency, they'll take the clutch gene that has delivered seven RBI, including two that snatched victory from the jaws of defeat.
1B Jake Bauers
There were 137 players who took at least 500 plate appearances this season, and only 12 of them had a better OPS+ than Bauers. Not bad for a 31-year-old who had an 84 OPS+ for his career coming into the season.
Bauers has become a menace of another sort in the playoffs. Even if he only has one multi-hit game, he's shown tremendous patience in racking up a .441 OBP and driving in six runs. He had multiple at-bats that dug the Los Angeles Dodgers' grave as he was winning MVP honors for the NLCS.
C William Contreras
Contreras has regressed a little as a regular-season performer, but you'd never know from how he's hit this postseason. He's hit safely in six of eight games, with three home runs and five RBI.
Also, don't overlook his mastery of the ABS. He challenged a league-high 185 calls from behind the plate this season, and he won 80 of them. He's kept it up in the playoffs, going 8-for-12 and winning some truly game-changing challenges.
RHP Jacob Misiorowski
After making 30 starts and pitching to a 1.80 ERA and a 5.7 K/BB ratio, Misiorowski is going to win the NL Cy Young Award. As soon as he hit 104.8 mph on his first pitch of the playoffs, he seemed ready to tap into still another gear for October.
Except, he hasn't made it past the fifth inning in either of his two assignments, consisting of nine hits and four walks in 8.1 total innings. He clearly isn't gassed, but he'll need to be better to maximize Milwaukee's chances in the World Series.
LHP Aaron Ashby
Milwaukee's entire bullpen has been incredible in the playoffs, handling 40.2 innings and allowing just six earned runs. Trevor Megill and Abner Uribe deserve their flowers, too.
Yet Ashby has simply been on another level, thus far posting 12.1 shutout innings and allowing just four hits and three walks. The next hitter who gets a knock off his curveball, changeup or slider will be the first.
Matchups That Will Define the World Series
4 of 6
Junior Caminero's Bat Speed vs. the Brewers' Velocity
What makes Caminero so dangerous? For one thing, nobody whips the bat through the zone like he does. His average swing this season was 79.5 mph, the highest of any qualified hitter.
In the World Series, though, he'll be up against a Brewers pitching staff that is averaging 98.3 mph on the fastball. That's almost a full mile per hour faster than the hardest-throwing staff of the 2025 playoffs.
Chandler Simpson's Speed vs. the Brewers' Defenders
Simpson is basically a free 90 feet in human form. He had 11 more infield hits than anyone else this season. He also stole 46 bases, and took 21 more bases on wild pitches, passed balls and the like. It all makes him a rare weapon.
The Brewers, though, could be up to stopping him. Their infield was among the very best this season with a total output of +7 Outs Above Average. More to the point, William Contreras was second in the league in caught-stealings.
Jacob Misiorowski vs. the Rays' High-Contact Offense
Misiorowski's contact rate during the regular season was a mere 65.5 percent, easily the best in baseball. Yet he hasn't been nearly as successful at avoiding contact in the postseason, where his rate has jumped to 77.4 percent.
If the San Diego Padres and Los Angeles Dodgers could do that, the Rays should be able to as well. They led MLB with an 81.8 contact percentage during the regular season, and it has only gone down to 77.2 in the postseason.
The Brewers' Lefty Bats vs. the Rays' Righty-Heavy Pitching
It isn't just Jake Bauers. Milwaukee's left-handed hitters as a collective have a 122 wRC+ in the playoffs, and that's despite facing some darn good left-handed pitching. In the NLCS alone, they faced a pair of two-time Cy Young Award winners in Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell.
The Rays aren't nearly as synonymous with left-handed pitching, indeed carrying only three for the ALCS against Cleveland. And one of them (Ian Seymour) isn't looking so hot after carrying a heavy workload in the regular season.
X-Factors That Will Define the World Series
5 of 6
Home Cooking
The best home record in MLB during the regular season? Well, it was a tie at 55-26… between the Rays and Brewers, naturally.
Neither club has fumbled its home-field advantage in the postseason. The Brewers are 4-0 at American Family Field. The Rays are 4-1 at Tropicana Field. So on paper, both teams can claim to have an advantage on their home turf.
That said, it's the Brewers who truly stand to find out. If this series goes the distance, they'll have the honor of hosting the finale in Milwaukee on October 31.
The Three True Outcomes
For the uninitiated, the three true outcomes are strikeouts, walks and home runs. Neither the Rays nor the Brewers was necessarily synonymous with the concept during the regular season, specifically in the sense that they both ranked in the bottom 10 of the league in home runs.
They have since gone on wildly different paths in October. The Brewers' percentage of three true outcomes when on offense is at 47 percent. For the Rays, it's only 31 percent.
Both paths have ultimately arrived in the same spot, but this may be where we find out which one wins the day. Can the Brewers keep winning by racking up walks and homers? Or, will the Rays avoid enough strikeouts to gain the inside track?
Speed and Defense
Regardless of what happens in the TTO department, neither of these teams should be expected to give much away, while both should be expected to take as much as they can get.
In other words, they're both good at fielding the ball and running the bases. The Rays and Brewers each ranked in the top six for defensive efficiency this season. They were both top-five in stolen bases, and separated by just two steals in the end.
In these respects, the World Series should reward baseball purists for their attention. The result could come down to fine margins—a ball just out of reach or a tag applied just in time.
Predicting the Outcome and World Series MVP
6 of 6
For the World Series: Brewers in 6
Regarding my credentials, I had the Brewers sweeping the Dodgers in the NLCS before it happened. So, I've been right at least once in my life.
Yet whereas the Dodgers looked old, slow and generally out of sorts while trying to keep pace with Milwaukee, the Rays are cut from the same cloth as a ballclub. They're younger and more athletic, and committed to playing smart, clean baseball that emphasizes the little things to add up to one big haymaker.
One area where Milwaukee should have an edge is on offense. The Brewers have as many as five hitters you really have to worry about. The Rays really only have three, in Junior Caminero, Yandy Díaz and Jonathan Aranda.
The Brewers' bullpen stands out as another advantage, even if they'll need more from their starters to avoid their relievers getting overexposed in a longer series. It, too, is deeper than what the Rays have to offer. And let's be real that Milwaukee relievers are simply on a heater right now.
So, congratulations in advance to the Brewers. If anything is worth a 57-year wait, it's a World Series championship.
For World Series MVP: William Contreras
This pick is partially about deferring to a hot hand. The Brewers have gotten contributions from all their hitters in the postseason, but Contreras has been a constant the whole way through. You just can't fake a 1.157 OPS.
Between his ABS challenges and his ability to control the running game, Contreras' defense also stands to be a huge factor in the World Series. He could also be a not-so-secret weapon when Freddy Peralta pitches for the Rays. If anyone knows him, it's the guy who caught him 81 times between 2023 and 2025.
