The 2026 MLB Postseason is entering the Championship Series, but the time for fantasy baseball analysis never truly stops. Last Monday, we started our Rotoworld Staff and Friends Fantasy Baseball Mock Draft for the 2027 season. While many places do a “too early” mock draft, we’d argue that it’s not really too early to look ahead to next season. I’ve been posting a collection of “look back” articles reviewing the best picks of the 2026 season, the worst picks, and my key lessons, but all of these articles are linked together by the idea that immediately taking stock in the season, before the offseason hype starts to creep in, can be an incredibly valuable experience.
So we invited our staff and a few of our friends to put together a 15-round mock draft that we’ll complete over the next couple of weeks and continue to break down for you in chunks over on our site. Today you’ll get the first four rounds, and then I’ll be back to update the next four or five rounds by the end of the week and then do one more update at the end.
We hope you find it a useful tool, and we’ll see how much it changes over the next few weeks.
2027 Fantasy Baseball Mock Draft
| Round 1 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 1 | RotoPat (Rotoworld) | Shohei Ohtani | UT/SP | LAD |
| 2 | George Bissell (Rotoworld) | Pete Crow-Armstrong | OF | CHC |
| 3 | Frank Stampfl (CBS Sports) | Bobby Witt Jr. | SS | KC |
| 4 | D.J. Short (Rotoworld) | Elly De La Cruz | SS | CIN |
| 5 | Scott Pianowski (Yahoo Sports) | Fernando Tatis Jr. | 2B/OF | SD |
| 6 | Rivers McCown (Rotoworld) | Junior Caminero | 3B | TB |
| 7 | Matthew Pouliot (Rotoworld) | Aaron Judge | OF | NYY |
| 8 | Dave Shovein (Rotoworld) | Juan Soto | OF | NYM |
| 9 | Frank Ammirante (RotoBaller) | Jackson Chourio | OF | MIL |
| 10 | James Schiano (Rotoworld) | James Wood | OF | WSH |
| 11 | Justin Mason (FanGraphs) | Yordan Alvarez | OF | HOU |
| 12 | Jorge Montanez (Rotoworld) | Ben Rice | 1B | NYY |
Perhaps the story here is that no starting pitchers went in the first 12 picks. One season after Tarik Skubal, Garrett Crochet, and Paul Skenes either got hurt or had down seasons, none of the drafters seemed willing to roll the dice on a starting pitcher with their first pick. Honestly, I can’t blame them. Early-round hitters, on average, continue to out-produce early-round pitchers at similar draft costs. The pitchers that do hit can make a huge difference for your team, but the risk is exponentially higher. A hitter taken here who fails to produce value, like Kyle Tucker this year, can still produce $10 of value, but a pitcher who goes in the first round and fails to produce value is almost always due to injury, and they can give you no value.
We did see Pat still choose Shohei Ohtani (dual position eligible here) as the top pick over Pete Crow-Armstrong. There are certainly some questions as to whether or not Ohtani’s body can hold up to a whole season as a starting pitcher and a DH, which will bring some uncertainty to his fantasy value. We also know he’s clearly not healthy right now, so we’ll need to see if any of these injuries require offseason surgery, but PCA has certainly worked his way into the conversation to be first overall.
A big surprise for some might be seeing Fernando Tatis Jr. this high. The Padres outfielder was one of the best hitters in baseball from June 1st on after a batting stance change allowed him to clear his hips more easily and unlock the pull-side power that we know he has. He also picked up 2B eligibility this season, which will be huge for him at a pretty barren position.
Jackson Chourio and James Wood have used breakout seasons to propel them into the first-round conversation, and you have to wonder if there is yet another level of development there, and Yordan Alvarez now has outfield eligibility in all formats, which makes him an even safer pick here. There look to be plenty of outfield options in the first round, including injured New York stars Juan Soto and Aaron Judge. Both of them being in the first round makes sense, but we may start to have to ask real questions about Judge’s durability. He’ll be 35 years old next season. He’s a giant human being, and the strain of playing the outfield every day at that size takes a real toll on your body. The fact that his two major injuries this season were both soft tissue or muscle injuries (and not a broken toe) should begin to raise some questions about whether or not we can count on 150+ games from Judge going forward.
His teammate, Ben Rice, used a 40-home run season to catapult him into the first round as well. That’s without catcher eligibility. Rice was the first 1B off the board in this draft, and I really find it hard to argue against that. Some guys in the next round have an argument, but Rice is a tremendous overall hitter. He has clear power. He plays in a great park for his approach, and there is no way the Yankees are going back to regularly sitting him against lefties. Even if Rice is more of a mid-30s home run hitter going forward than a true 40+ guy, his approach at the plate makes me feel good about his contact and batting average, and that puts him ahead of the guys who will follow him in round two.
| Round 2 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 13 | Jorge Montanez | CJ Abrams | SS/2B | WSH |
| 14 | Justin Mason | Jose Ramirez | 3B | CLE |
| 15 | James Schiano | Jacob Misiorowski | SP | MIL |
| 16 | Frank Ammirante | Tarik Skubal | SP | LAD |
| 17 | Dave Shovein | Ronald Acuña Jr. | OF | ATL |
| 18 | Matthew Pouliot | Nick Kurtz | 1B | OAK |
| 19 | Rivers McCown | Jordan Walker | OF | STL |
| 20 | Scott Pianowski | Kyle Schwarber | DH | PHI |
| 21 | D.J. Short | Pete Alonso | 1B | BAL |
| 22 | Frank Stampfl | Corbin Carroll | OF | ARI |
| 23 | George Bissell | Cam Schlittler | SP | NYY |
| 24 | Roto Pat | Yoshinobu Yamamoto | SP | LAD |
And now the pitchers start to come off the board. Not really a surprise with who the first three arms were off the board: Jacob Misiorowski, Tarik Skubal, and Cam Schlittler. I assume those will be the top three arms in pretty much all rankings heading into 2027. Pat did snag Yoshinobu Yamamoto as the fourth starter picked in this round, and while some may argue for Chris Sale or Cristopher Sanchez here, there’s a strong case that Yamamoto could be locked into the fourth spot. There is still some elevated risk with starting pitchers in the second round, but at least every one of these teams added an elite bat in the first round, and both George and Pat were able to take second elite bats at the start of the third round, so this risk feels more palatable.
CJ Abrams is another player, like Tatis Jr., who picked up second base eligibility in most formats. That’s huge for his fantasy value. So is hitting .261 with 33 home runs and 34 steals while driving in 106 runs. Abrams will be 26 years old next season, and while his future in Washington is a bit cloudy, he’s an elite offensive talent who is finally making good on that promise.
We had some former first-round picks fall into the second with Jose Ramirez, Ronald Acuña Jr., and Corbin Carroll all falling into the second round. The falls make sense too. Ramirez and Acuña Jr. now just have a bit more injury risk than some of the other players going in the first round. Ramirez still has great upside at a position that lacks talent, which may drive his price up, but he’ll be 34 years old, and he hit just 12 home runs and batted .235 this year after hamate surgery. Are you willing to bet that he gets back to 100% of his old self, or do we think it’s more likely that he’ll be 75-80% of the guy who almost went 40/40 in 2024? Acuña Jr. is a harder bet because he has now played under 108 games in three straight seasons and has played over 120 games once since 2019. It’s hard to bet on a full season of production, and with PCA, Chourio, and James Wood emerging, it makes sense to go with the younger/healthier players.
At the same position, the most interesting name in this round is probably Jordan Walker. He had a breakout season this year, hitting .269 with 29 home runs, 102 RBI, and 22 steals. He also just turned 24 years old, so there is plenty of growth still possible for him. He struggled through an injury at the end of the year, which hurt his September stats, but there will be no half measures with Walker in 2027. You have to either be all-in on the fact that 2026 was a real breakout for a former top prospect or just acknowledge that you won’t be getting him in your drafts.
Pete Alonso and Nick Kurtz are the two first basemen I alluded to earlier who land here in round 2. Kurtz played just 99 games this season due to injury but still hit 21 home runs while batting .256. We know the hitting environment in Sacramento is elite, so he should still be going in this range.
| Round 3 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 25 | Roto Pat | Sal Stewart | 1B | CIN |
| 26 | George Bissell | Konnor Griffin | SS | PIT |
| 27 | Frank Stampfl | Miguel Vargas | 3B | CHW |
| 28 | D.J. Short | Cristopher Sanchez | SP | PHI |
| 29 | Scott Pianowski | Paul Skenes | SP | PIT |
| 30 | Rivers McCown | Mason Miller | RP | SD |
| 31 | Matthew Pouliot | Julio Rodriguez | OF | SEA |
| 32 | Dave Shovein | Trea Turner | SS | PHI |
| 33 | Frank Ammirante | Gunnar Henderson | SS | BAL |
| 34 | James Schiano | Jackson Merrill | OF | SD |
| 35 | Justin Mason | Kevin McGonigle | SS/3B | DET |
| 36 | Jorge Montanez | Jesus Luzardo | SP | PHI |
We see three current-year rookies go in Round 3, announcing themselves as top-tier talents for years to come, and it’s hard to argue against it. Sal Stewart, Konnor Griffin, and Kevin McGonigle all showed that they can handle this level of competition, and we should expect more growth from these young players. The same goes for Miguel Vargas, who is not a rookie but broke out in 2026 in a way that suggests consistent value. He’s always had an elite plate approach, and now he added pull-side power to that equation. Vargas will be 27 years old and is in an ascending lineup, so he belongs in this range.
We saw the next group of starting pitchers go with Cristopher Sanchez, Paul Skenes, and Jesus Luzardo. Obviously, the name everybody will want to talk about is Skenes. It was a bad year for the Pirates ace, and while he claimed he wasn’t hurt, his velocity fell throughout the year, and he was not missing as many bats. There had been some previous concerns that his fastball wasn’t a huge whiff pitch to righties (10.7% swinging strike rate in 2025), but Skenes saw huge strides there this season. However, that was basically the only place he got better, and by elevating his four-seamer more for whiffs, he also started to allow more hard contact. It’s hard to see Skenes being this bad again, but we also can’t ignore how this season went.
Mason Miller went here as the first closer off the board, and three former first-round picks fell in Gunnar Henderson, Trea Turner, and Julio Rodriguez. I covered Gunnar and Trea in my article on what I learned from the 2026 fantasy baseball season, so you should read that, but essentially their 2025 price baked in a full return to peak value and ignored the warning signs from that season. We don’t appear to be doing that this year.
| Round 4 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 37 | Jorge Montanez | Drew Rasmussen | SP | TB |
| 38 | Justin Mason | Chris Sale | SP | ATL |
| 39 | James Schiano | Francisco Lindor | SS | NYM |
| 40 | Frank Ammirante | Kyle Tucker | OF | LAD |
| 41 | Dave Shovein | Brice Turang | 2B | MIL |
| 42 | Matthew Pouliot | Zach Neto | SS | LAA |
| 43 | Rivers McCown | Oneil Cruz | OF | PIT |
| 44 | Scott Pianowski | Matt Olson | 1B | ATL |
| 45 | D.J. Short | Carson Benge | OF | NYM |
| 46 | Frank Stampfl | Chase Burns | SP | CIN |
| 47 | George Bissell | Hunter Goodman | C | COL |
| 48 | Roto Pat | Nolan McLean | SP | NYM |
Now we answer the question of how far Kyle Tucker falls as Frank Ammirante takes him with the fourth pick in the fourth round, 40th overall. I covered Tucker more extensively in my article revisiting the top two rounds of 2025 drafts, but the miss on Tucker was essentially looking at pedigree (his seasons before his last two injured ones) and also the team context (a move to the Dodgers) and ignoring that he hadn’t had a fully productive year in a while. I’m not sure anybody expected that Tucker would see his barrel-rate collapse and that he would make uncharacteristically aggressive, out-of-character swing decisions, so perhaps we can expect a slight bounce back to his previously healthy form.
Four more starting pitchers go off the board here, and it’s an interesting group. Drew Rasmussen was brilliant this season, but it was also his first over 150 innings, and he’s had three elbow surgeries. Can you bank on his health as your ace? Kind of the same question for Chris Sale, who will be 38 next year and has basically alternated healthy years with injured years. After being hurt for basically all of 2021-23, he threw 178 innings in 2024, then 125 in 2025, and then 163 this year. What’s in store for 2027?
The final two arms were young pitchers in Chase Burns and Nolan McLean. The Burns pick makes sense given his elite strikeout upside and plus raw stuff, but McLean is harder to see here. Not that he’s a bad pitcher, but taking him as the 11th starting pitcher is assuming tons of growth. His 26% strikeout rate and 16.6% K-BB% don’t line up with some of the elite arms in this range, and his 10.5% swinging strike rate continues to suggest some concern with his ability to consistently miss bats. He’ll be 26 next year, and he’s clearly a talented arm, but taking him this high means he really HAS to take the next step, or he won’t return value.
Oneil Cruz’s bounce-back season pushed him up into the fourth round, and he’s joined by young outfielder Carson Benge, who hit .282 with 20 home runs and 22 steals in his rookie season. He didn’t get the fanfare of the other rookies who went higher in this draft, but Benge has a true five-category skill set and should be in an improved lineup next season.
We also saw our first catcher go off the board in Hunter Goodman. Keep in mind that this is a one-catcher format, which is why you’re not seeing a lot of catchers go early, but George wanted to lock up an elite bat at the position. With Ben Rice no longer catcher eligible, Goodman was the top fantasy catcher this season after hitting 41 home runs, driving in 88 runs, and hitting .245 in Coors Field. There’s little reason to believe he can’t do it again.
| Round 5 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 49 | Roto Pat | Rafael Devers | 1B | SF |
| 50 | George Bissell | Cade Smith | RP | CLE |
| 51 | Frank Stampfl | Zack Wheeler | SP | PHI |
| 52 | D.J. Short | Parker Messick | SP | CLE |
| 53 | Scott Pianowski | Randy Arozarena | OF | SEA |
| 54 | Rivers McCown | Dylan Cease | SP | TOR |
| 55 | Matthew Pouliot | Vladimir Guerrero Jr. | 1B | TOR |
| 56 | Dave Shovein | Logan Gilbert | SP | SEA |
| 57 | Frank Ammirante | Garrett Crochet | SP | BOS |
| 58 | James Schiano | Bryce Harper | 1B/OF | PHI |
| 59 | Justin Mason | Logan Henderson | SP | MIL |
| 60 | Jorge Montanez | Michael Harris II | OF | ATL |
A few big-name starting pitchers with major injuries go in this round. Zack Wheeler (SP12) missed half of this past season after having thoracic outlet surgery, Garrett Crochet (SP16) missed basically the whole season with a shoulder injury, Dylan Cease (SP14) ended the season on the injured list with a shoulder injury, and Logan Henderson (SP17) has missed time in each of the last two seasons with injuries. We’re now outside of the top 10 starting pitchers, so these guys don’t HAVE to be your ace, but this is still an early round draft pick for pitchers who have some overall health concerns. I understand the argument for their upside, and while I may not make the pick here, that’s just my personal drafting philosophy.
Parker Messick (SP13) and Logan Gilbert (SP15) also go in this round. Both of them feel a bit safer from a health standpoint, and there is still an argument that Gilbert has another level of production to hit. I have him as a top-10 starting pitcher, so I like him going as the 15th starter off the board.
We see Cade Smith go here as the second closer off the board, and Rafael Devers and Bryce Harper make sense in this range as veteran 1B who are likely past their peak but continue to produce overall solid numbers. Devers really turned things around after a slow start to the year and seems as consistent as ever.
We also see two outfielders coming off big seasons in Michael Harris II and Randy Arozarena. James Schiano and I actually discussed this exact either-or in a video we recorded after the Braves were eliminated from the postseason. I picked Harris II easily because I believe in the changes he’s made over the last year-and-a-half, and I’m not looking to pay for Arozarena’s career year.
Lastly, we need to address Vladimir Guerrero Jr., who finally goes off the board here in the fifth. We all know how Vlad Jr. struggled this year, but he’s now going as the sixth 1B, late in the fifth round, which is way more palatable for me. I know the power wasn’t there, but we have enough of a track record to feel confident that he is at least a 20-25 home run bat who can hit .280 in what should be a solid lineup. That’s still a solid fantasy asset; it’s just not a pick to make in the first three rounds of your draft. Also, getting corrective eye surgery can’t be bad either.
| Round 6 | | | | |
| Pick | Manager | Player | POS | Team |
| 61 | Jorge Montanez | Jac Caglianone | OF | KC |
| 62 | Justin Mason | Jhoan Duran | RP | PHI |
| 63 | James Schiano | Jazz Chisholm Jr. | OF | NYY |
| 64 | Frank Ammirante | Cal Raleigh | C | SEA |

This is a super interesting round to me, and I can’t make much sense of it, haha. There seem to be no runs here or any real trend.
We do get more catchers off the board here with Cal Raleigh, Drake Baldwin, and Shea Langeliers. It feels a little early to be in a one-catcher format, but everybody has their own strategy. Baldwin feels like a great pick after his 2026 season, and while I do think Raleigh is going to bounce back after a down 2026 season, I’m not sure he’d be the gamble I take this early in the sixth round. Yes, you might be getting 30+ home runs from that spot, but the batting average will be a drain, and we have no idea if that lineup will be any good.
Jhoan Duran goes off the board as the third closer, and then Andres Munoz next was a bit of a surprise. He wasn’t really in a closer committee in Seattle this year; they just didn’t get a lot of saves. His SIERA and underlying metrics look a lot better than his ERA, so it does feel like he was just unlucky, but I’m not that convinced the Mariners will be that good next year, and Munoz has never delivered as a consistent top 5-8 closer.
Three risky hitters with plenty of upside also go in this round: Jac Caglianone, Jazz Chisholm Jr., and Wyatt Langford. We don’t really know where Jazz will be next year, but it seems like it won’t be New York. That’s likely a big park downgrade for him. His batting average also regressed pretty drastically this season, which had been a concern for him in previous years. We know the speed will always be there, so he’ll need to land in a park where the power can come as well, but this feels like a fair spot for him. Caglianone is also a popular breakout pick because his batted ball data has been really strong. I like the idea of him taking a big step next season, but a top-60 pick does feel like you’re paying as if the breakthrough is a given. We all know the deal with Langford at this point too. A top-70 pick on him feels right if he can stay healthy, but can he ever stay healthy?
Bryan Woo at SP18 and Gavin Williams at SP19 feel like strong picks at this point. Both of them have immense strikeout upside and the ability to be top-10 starting pitchers. Woo had a bad stretch this season but seemed to right the ship at the end of the year, and Williams still seems to have one iffy inning every game where his command gets wonky. However, the big surprise here was Kade Anderson. I know he was an elite pitching prospect, but he doesn’t have elite MLB velocity or Stuff+, which means that he gets by with command and a deep enough pitch mix. I think he will be a solid starting pitcher, but I’m not sure I see the ceiling to take him as SP20, especially in what will be his rookie season.

Round 7 gave us quite the run on outfielders. After Wyatt Langford ended last round, Henry Bolte, Riley Greene, Andy Pages, Ceddanne Rafaela, Byron Buxton, and Seiya Suzuki all came off the board in the seventh round. Bolte is the name that probably stands out. The Athletics’ rookie hit .277/.359/.405 in 119 big league games with 11 home runs and 21 steals. In 65 games in the second half, Bolte hit .289/.370/.448 with eight of his home runs and a 9.2% barrel rate. Bolte has always had loud raw tools, but he has struggled to lift the ball consistently, which has limited his power output. We started to see that a little more from him in the second half and, if it carries over, he has the makings of a 20/30 hitter in a great ballpark. Pat taking him at 73 means Bolte kind of HAS to get close to that in order to return value, which makes the pick a bit of a risk but not one without some logic to it.
The Buxton and Suzuki picks have their own risk too, along with clear upside. Buxton, who was coming off his best season in years, was limited to just 93 games because of a hip injury that ultimately required surgery. He’ll be 33 years old next season, with just one season over 105 games played since 2017 and coming off major hip surgery. A bit on him inside the top 80 is a huge risk, but we also know Buxton can produce fantasy value in 80-100 games. Suzuki is less of an injury risk but more of a team context risk since we have no idea where he’ll be playing next year. Perhaps it could provide a boost to his home run potential. Maybe the team context will limit his counting stats. We won’t know that for a while.
Two more starting pitchers also go here in Max Fried (SP21) and Payton Tolle (SP22), and, spoiler alert, one of them looks like a huge steal. When my starting pitching rankings come out later this week, I will have Tolle in my top 10 starting pitchers. He’ll be slotted right ahead of a tier of aces who have a history of injury (Crochet, Sale, deGrom, Wheeler), so maybe you want to call Tolle a top 15 starter if you’d take all of those injury risks over him. Still, getting a potential top 15 starting pitcher with pick 82 is tremendous. In case you think top-15 is rich for Tolle, he finished as the SP25 this season, and that was while recording just nine wins in 26 starts. He had a 3.03 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, and 28.4% strikeout rate and will be just 24 years old next season. As his breaking balls continue to develop, his performance should only improve.

After Josh Hader went off the board in the last round as RP5, we got a run on closers here in the eighth round with Aroldis Chapman (RP6), Louis Varland (RP7), Mason Montgomery (RP8), Bryan Baker (RP9), and Grant Taylor (RP10). Hader and Chapman are the two established names among the group and make clear sense here, and Baker tied for the MLB lead in saves this season and will return for the potential World Series champion Rays. I’d say that makes him a solid top-ten closer. The other three are all bets on upside, and all bets that make sense. Varland was electric as a closer for the Blue Jays this season and finished as RP3 on the year. Taylor and Montgomery weren’t even full-time closers, and they finished as RP6 and RP7, respectively, due to their high innings totals and strikeout rates. The potential issue for both Taylor and Montgomery is that we have no idea if they will be used as traditional closers. Montgomery feels like the better bet since he had 18 saves this season, but it also took the Pirates a while to turn the role over to him, and they may prefer him in the “fireman” role in the same way the White Sox seem to prefer Taylor. That said, both of them are dominant relief arms.
Three young hitters also went in this round with Zack Gelof, Chase DeLauter, and JJ Wetherholt. Wetherholt as a top 100 pick after his rookie season makes sense, and DeLauter also clearly has the profile of a top 10 pick. His issue has been, and always will be, health risk. Yet, he did manage to play 133 games this season, hitting .287/.363/.457 with 16 home runs and 11 steals. The hard-hit rates suggest that more power could be coming if he can lift the ball a bit more consistently.
Jorge’s pick of Gelof is also a bet that the 26-year-old really did reinvent himself this season, when he hit .256/.322/.475 with 22 home runs and 16 steals in 111 games. Gelof chased less outside of the zone, took a more patient approach overall, made more contact than he ever has, and was less pull-happy than he had been previously. All of that seems to suggest very real growth. Can the growth hold? That will be the big question you have to ask yourself if you draft him in the top 85 picks next season.
We also saw Hunter Brown go off the board here as SP23. If you had told people in March that you’d get Hunter Brown near the end of the eighth round, it would have seemed like a major coup. However, the Astros ace returned from a shoulder injury this season and never looked like himself. Is the injury still lingering, or was 2025 a bit of a fluke? Remember that he had a 3.49 ERA, 1.27 WHIP, and 25% strikeout rate in 2024. There was a major jump forward in 2025, but much of that was in the first half of the season. Even though his ratios remained strong after the All-Star break in 2025, his strikeout rate fell to 24%. So maybe Brown is more of a low 3.00-ERA pitcher who will post a 26% strikeout rate. That’s not a bad profile, but it’s not a top 15 arm. Then you have the health questions to factor in as well, so his slide here makes a bit of sense to me.

item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays — the top team in the American League — has held its own to achieve the third pennant in franchise history, and their second this decade.
The Milwaukee Brewers are back in the World Series for the first time since 1982, and they're doing it as the National League's best team. The 103-win Crew swept the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS and now host the Tampa Bay Rays in a matchup of two franchise-first title seekers. Game 1 is Friday at American Family Field.
Here's a position-by-position look at the Brewers as they prepare for the Rays.
Catcher
William Contreras is the lead backstop for Milwaukee, and one of the most popular Brewers, as he has been one of the more reliable all-around catchers in the National League in recent years and in the playoffs, as his bat has stayed productive into October. He posted a strong 1.157 OPS with three homers through the NLCS while handling a staff that mixes elite velocity with a deep lefty presence.
At backup, the more familiar Gary Sánchez provides a power-oriented option off the bench.
Infield
The Brewers' infield blends elite defense, speed, and opportunistic offense.
- First base: Jake Bauers. The NLCS MVP has been the postseason story for Milwaukee. A well-known Rays prospect if you've read this site for any length of time, Bauers nearly retired but returned for what he considered one more season last year to keep his health insurance benefits after his wife became pregnant with their second child. Fast forward two seasons, and he has delivered lengthy at bats with power and timely hitting throughout October while providing solid enough defense at the corner. Veteran White Sox infielder Andrew Vaughn has also seen time at first and as a right-handed bat off the bench or at DH against lefties.
- Second base: Brice Turang. One of the best all-around second basemen in baseball and the No. 2 hitter. Turang combines Gold Glove-caliber defense with improved power (21 home runs and 100 RBIs in the regular season) and baserunning. He's a clear mismatch advantage and not to be trifled with.
- Shortstop: Cooper Pratt. The 22-year old rookie shortstop has started the bulk of the postseason games. He's shown a contact-oriented approach and improving glove work as the year has progressed, and pushing the previous starter Ortiz into a third base platoon.
- Third base: Joey Ortiz / David Hamilton. This has been a platoon/mix-and-match spot. The right handed hitting Ortiz and left handed hitting Hamilton now split time depending on matchups. If we are drawing comparisons, neither matches Junior Caminero's power, but both offer speed and defensive flexibility that fits Milwaukee's style.
Outfield
Milwaukee's outfield is built on athleticism, defense, and a rising star.
- Left field: Jackson Chourio. This 22-year-old superstar has continued his rapid ascent in 2026. Already with multiple 20-20 seasons under his belt, Chourio brings power, speed, and improving defense. He's the dynamic centerpiece of the lineup, their version of a Junior Caminero, and fun to watch.
- Center field: Garrett Mitchell. Strong defensive center fielder who has delivered several big hits in the playoffs, including a go-ahead home run in the NLCS clincher. He gets on base and covers ground.
- Right field: Sal Frelick. Elite defender with speed and contact skills. Luis Lara has spelled him against left-handers and provides another athletic option. The group ranks among the best defensive outfields in the league.
Technically also an outfielder, the Designated Hitter, Christian Yelich, remains in the lineup and was recently named club captain. While not at his peak production levels, his experience and ability to still impact games remain valuable, especially against right-handed pitching.
Rotation
Manager Pat Murphy has utilized short leashes and heavy bullpen support, but has a solid rotation heading into the World Series:
- Jacob Misiorowski — The clear ace and yet to be crowned NL Cy Young winner (16-5, 1.80 ERA, 252 strikeouts in the regular season). He's started Game 1 of both the NLDS and NLCS and will surely open the World Series. To say his high-velocity stuff that ranks among the best is an understatement. I half expected Misiorowski to mean fast in Polish, but apparently it's something closer to bear.
- Logan Henderson — The reliable No. 2. Solid second-half performer who has handled Game 2 duties effectively in his sophomore season as a homegrown talent.
- Robert Gasser — Emerged as the preferred Game 3 option after strong late-season form and solid postseason outings (including shutout work in the NLCS). He was acquired in the Josh Hader trade with San Diego, over came a UCL surgery in 2025, and started the year in Triple-A, making his rise a bit unexpected. His dad's best friend is evidently Vin Diesel.
- Dustin May (with Shane Drohan as an Opener) — May has postseason experience but has been used carefully; Florida State alumni Drohan opened Game 4 in the NLCS, and the southpaw seems likely to get the nod again given how well that went last time.
No starter has gone particularly deep in October, which is by design. Milwaukee trusts its relievers to take over after four or five innings, limiting any time-through-the-order penalties.
Bullpen
This unit has been the difference-maker. The Brewers' bullpen allowed just six earned runs across more than 40 postseason innings heading into the World Series and featured relievers earning the win in all four NLCS games during the sweep of Los Angeles.
- Trevor Megill — 6'8" Closer. Reliable late-inning presence, and a bit of an invention by the Brewers, having been added for a PTBNL in April 2023.
- Abner Uribe — Primary setup man. High-velocity right-hander who has been outstanding, despite blowing a save in Game 3 of the NLCS he's been their best bullpen arm this month.
- Aaron Ashby — Left-handed workhorse who has been nearly unhittable in October (multiple scoreless multi-inning outings) and got the save in Game 4 of the sweep.
- DL Hall / JoJo Romero — Additional lefty depth options that each were credited wins in the NLCS.
Regular season starter Kyle Harrison will likely find his way into the mix as well. The group throws exceptionally hard on average and enters the series fully rested after the NLCS sweep and the Rays' longer ALCS.
Conclusion
The Brewers' formula is clear: elite defense, contact and speed on offense, an electric frontline starter, and a lights-out bullpen that can cover the middle and late innings.
Against a similarly constructed Rays team that also emphasizes pitching, defense, and small-ball elements, the series should be tight, low-scoring, and decided by the margins. Milwaukee holds home-field advantage and the deeper, harder-throwing relief corps—two factors that could prove decisive in a first-time-champion showdown.

Milwaukee Brewers superstar Jackson Chourio is the odds-on favorite to win the World Series MVP in the 2026 Fall Classic.
The Brewers advanced to the World Series for the first time since 1982, when they took down the mighty Los Angeles Dodgers, the reigning two-time World Series champions, with an eye-opening 4-0 sweep in the NLCS.
It was an absolutely incredible performance by the Brewers, who are now four wins away from capturing the first World Series championship in franchise history.
If they do end up winning it, then the oddsmakers like Chourio’s chances to be a big part of them doing so.
Jackson Chourio Is the World Series MVP Favorite
Per DraftKings Sportsbook, Chourio is the odds-on favorite to win the World Series MVP award this season.
Chourio is currently at +600 odds, putting him just ahead of his Brewers teammates, C William Contreras at +650, SP Jacob Misiorowski at +700, and 2B Brice Turang at +900, to capture this year’s World Series MVP award.
Since the ALCS between the Cleveland Guardians and the Tampa Bay Rays has not yet been decided, the odds will change from now until the start of the World Series one week from now.
Still, Chourio will be among the favorites to capture the World Series MVP award when the Brewers try to win the first championship in club history.
Jackson Chourio Is a Young Stud
Just 22 years old, Chourio is a young stud who has proven that he is one of the best young players in MLB since making his debut in 2024.
This season, Chourio hit .291 with a .837 OPS and a 129 OPS+ for the Brewers, indicating that his bat was 29% above league average.
He also belted 25 home runs and racked up 4.9 bWAR for the Brewers, along with stealing 23 bases.
Defensively, he had a strong year in LF and is a finalist for the Gold Glove Award.
During the postseason this year, Chourio has struggled a bit with just a .171 batting average, .553 OPS, and two home runs in eight games. But that is a very small sample size, and the oddsmakers know that he can turn it on at any moment.

item.content:encoded:
Milwaukee brings a commanding 3-0 lead into Game 4 of the National League Championship Series on Thursday night. But the Dodgers are the champs until they’re not, and they’ve faced plenty of adversity on their way to World Series titles in each of the past two seasons.
Never like this though. In all best-of-seven postseason series, teams with a 3-0 lead have gone on to win that series 41 times out of 42 -- with 32 of those series ending as sweeps. Only two teams have ever even forced a Game 7 after trailing 3-0, and only the 2004 Red Sox, in the ALCS against the Yankees, have come all the way back to win.
“It's certainly possible,” said Dodgers manager Dave Roberts, himself a fabled part of that Red Sox rally. “I've lived it. And I think the thing is that our guys have been battle-tested. … It's an elimination game. We've played in a lot of elimination games. We've just got to get a win.”
While the Dodgers chase baseball history, the Brewers can make a bit of their own with a win on Thursday. A year ago, they were swept by the Dodgers in the very same round. If they can return the favor, they would become the first team to be swept out of the playoffs, only to sweep the same team -- in any postseason series -- a year later. But they’re not getting ahead of themselves.
“We have yet to complete anything,” Brewers outfielder Jackson Chourio said through an interpreter. “The job's not finished for us. So we have to come with the same mentality. Which is to win.”
Here’s what you need to know about Game 4:
When is the game and how can I watch it?
Game 4 is currently airing nationally on FS1.
All series are available in the US on MLB.TV with authentication to a participating Pay TV provider. Games also are available live internationally, although not in Canada. Sportsnet is MLB's exclusive English language broadcaster in Canada for every Postseason game, while TVA Sports will be covering the entire AL Postseason and the World Series in French and Broadcaster RDS will cover the entire NL Postseason in French.
The Brewers picked Drohan from among a plethora of fresh options to start what amounts to a bullpen game. Left-handers Kyle Harrison and Drohan and right-hander Chad Patrick have been on the roster for both the NLDS and NLCS, but have yet to pitch in any of the Brewers’ first seven games. Midseason pickup Dustin May, the former Dodger who won a World Series ring with L.A. in 2020, pitched an inning in NLCS Game 2 on what would have been a bullpen day had he been lined up to start Thursday. They are all options to come in behind Drohan, who had a 4.19 ERA in 33 games/19 starts and shifted to the bullpen late in the season when he came upon a loose innings limit. He thrived in short stints, posting a 1.47 ERA as a reliever. It will be his career postseason debut.
The Dodgers' 7-0 postseason record when Glasnow pitches is more of a quirk than anything else, but the right-hander has gotten the results to back it up. In four starts and three relief appearances, Glasnow has recorded a 1.73 ERA (five earned runs in 26 innings). Glasnow had command issues when he last pitched against the Braves in NLDS Game 4 -- issuing five walks -- but limited the damage to one run in 4 2/3 innings.
What are the starting lineups?
Brewers: The lineup the Brewers used against right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto in Game 2 produced the second postseason game in franchise history in which five different players tallied multiple hits. Against Glasnow in Game 4, they hope for a similar result with the same group.
Dodgers: Not only are the Dodgers sticking with Shohei Ohtani despite his lingering right biceps and left knee issues, they're bumping him up to leadoff for a must-win game. He and a scuffling Will Smith -- batting cleanup for Game 4 -- were dropped in the lineup in the past couple games, but the fact that both contributed to L.A.'s lone run-scoring rally in Game 3 likely played a role in Roberts' decision to elevate them Thursday.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Brewers: Right-handed setup man Abner Uribe, who has appeared in each of the first seven games of the postseason, finally wilted a bit in Game 3, walking three batters ahead of Smith’s two-run double in the sixth inning. But left-hander DL Hall kept the game on track by stopping the rally there and recording seven enormous outs. Then Trevor Megill logged a four-out save. That’s a lot of work for those last two arms, so lefty Aaron Ashby figures to play a prominent role in Game 4 if the score is tight.
Dodgers: It's all hands on deck, with the possible exception of Justin Wrobleski, who threw 32 pitches to cover the final 1 2/3 innings of Game 3. Roberts made a point of saying that he will get closer Edwin Díaz --- the only Dodgers reliever who has not pitched this series -- into Game 4.
Any injuries of note?
Brewers: None.
Dodgers: Ohtani (right biceps, left knee) and Freeman (right knee) are managing lingering injuries. World Series hero Will Klein (right elbow discomfort) has faced hitters, but he has not pitched in a game since July 31 and is viewed as more of a depth option. Blake Treinen (right shoulder inflammation) is unlikely to pitch this postseason.
Who is hot and who is not?
Brewers: Chourio’s .642 OPS in this postseason doesn’t tell anything about his impact. His leadoff home run in Game 3 marked his second homer of the 2026 postseason and sixth of his career, breaking a brief tie with William Contreras for the most homers in Brewers’ postseason history. Three of them have led off a postseason game, which matched Hall of Famer Derek Jeter, Jimmy Rollins and Ohtani for the second-most in history, trailing only Kyle Schwarber, who has five leadoff home runs in the postseason. And with his 18th career postseason RBI, Chourio also broke a tie with Hall of Famer Andruw Jones for the most postseason RBIs prior to a player’s 23rd birthday. … With his eighth-inning base hit, Contreras became the first Brewers player with 10 hits in this postseason.
Dodgers: Tucker (.304) has consistently swung the bat well through seven games, but he has been the exception to the rule for a cold Dodgers offense. In Game 3, Ohtani (113.5 mph single) and Smith (two-run double) showed some positive signs, but they have been L.A.'s most notable slumping bats this postseason.
Anything else fans might want to know?
•  Orel Hershiser and Mike Scioscia will throw out the ceremonial first pitch and say, "It's time for Dodger baseball!" as part of the pregame ceremonies.
• According to the Elias Sports Bureau, this is the eighth time two teams met in the postseason one year after one swept the other in the previous postseason. The only team to be swept and then win a rematch the following postseason is the 1923 Yankees, who won that year's World Series over the New York Giants in six games.
• Brewers owner Mark Attanasio said it struck him that it’s been 44 years since the Brewers made it to the World Series, and 44 is one of the franchise’s retired numbers for Hall of Famer Hank Aaron. This year marked the 50th anniversary of Aaron’s 755th and final home run, which he hit while playing for the Brewers in 1976.
• This marks the sixth time a team has taken a 3-0 series lead against the reigning World Series champion in a best-of-seven series. Four of the previous five -- 1990 WS, Reds vs A’s; 1966 WS, Orioles vs Dodgers; 1963 WS, Dodgers vs Yankees; 1914 WS, Boston Braves vs Philadelphia Athletics -- ended in a sweep. The other (2017 NLCS, Dodgers vs Cubs) concluded with the Dodgers winning in five games.

LOS ANGELES – Pat Murphy clearly had bigger fish to fry on Wednesday, Oct. 14 with his Milwaukee Brewers preparing to face the Los Angeles Dodgers in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series at Dodger Stadium.
But there was some Brewers-adjacent news that broke earlier in the day that irked Murphy – one of his best players had seemingly been disrespected.
William Contreras, whose 1,085 ⅔ innings and 9.064 pitches caught led the major leagues, was not among the three finalists at catcher in the National League for the Rawlings Gold Glove Award.
Those catchers were Freddy Fermin of the San Diego Padres, Gabriel Moreno of the Arizona Diamondbacks and Luis Torrens of the New York Mets.
"Contreras, he wasn't in there? Contreras?" said Murphy when asked initially for his reaction both to Brice Turang and Jackson Chourio being named finalists at second base and in left field, respectively, as well as any Brewers players he thought might have been snubbed.
"I'm biased. I get to see him 100-plus games catching. I think he caught the most games in the major leagues this year, and he was so important to us. They should come up with another award for William, because he's been incredible.
"So, if he's not on that list, ask for a redo."
The criteria is listed by Rawlings as the following:
To determine the winners of the 18 defensive position Awards, each team's manager and up to six coaches on his staff vote from a pool of qualified players in their League and cannot vote for players from their own team. In 2013, Rawlings added the SABR Defensive Index™ (SDI) to the Rawlings Gold Glove Award selection process, which comprises approximately 25 percent of the overall selection total, with the managers' and coaches' votes continuing to carry the majority.
To identify the utility Award winners, Rawlings collaborated with the Society for American Baseball Research (SABR) to create a specialized defensive formula separate from the traditional selection process for the Rawlings Gold Glove Award position winners. Utilizing the SABR formula and additional defensive statistics, Rawlings will select one utility winner from each League.
Looking at metrics, Contreras did rate out poorly in areas like framing (minus-6, 53rd out of 56 qualified catchers) and blocks above average (minus-7 on 4,361 opportunities). But with Contreras behind the plate, Brewers pitchers threw to a 3.32 ERA with the team ultimately going 80-41.
Contreras also threw out 28.4% of would-be basestealers (19 of 67).
Joey Ortiz also failed to make the cut as a utility player despite finishing 15th in the major leagues with 15 outs above average and also logged eight total defensive runs saved between third base and shortstop.
"Joey's a great defender," said Murphy. "I don't know the other guys in the league, but Joey, if given the chance to play every day on a team, you'd be hard-pressed to find a better defender. I don't know how all the voting takes place and everything. I know I vote, but I don't remember who was on there and who wasn't. You can't vote for your own players anyway.
"I try to just really vote for who I think is the best. I think you're doing a disservice if you try to like, 'Well, I don't want to vote for this guy because my guy's in competition.' I just voted for the guys that I think are the best. But for Contreras not to be on there, I don't know what it's based on. There's so many things in the catching position that you can't measure.
"So, now I'm kind of ticked about it now that you brought it up."

LOS ANGELES — The Brewers bullpen might be the biggest separating factor through two games of the National League Championship Series, with Milwaukee relievers combining for 9 2/3 scoreless innings thus far in the series.
Dodgers relievers were a strength of the team, and given the current health of the staff this might be the deepest postseason bullpen the team has had in recent years. During the postseason, the LA bullpen has a 3.13 ERA with 27 strikeouts and eight unintentional walks in 23 innings. In the NLCS, Dodgers relievers have allowed four runs in 8 1/3 innings but also have 15 strikeouts.
Dodgers batters have just two hits in 30 at-bats plus three walks against Brewers relievers in the series, unable to do anything late in the game. In Game 1, Los Angeles scored its only run in the second inning, and in Game 2 they didn't score after the fifth.
Aaron Ashby has pitched multiple innings in each game so far, totaling 3 2/3 innings. Abner Uribe was the other Brewer to pitch both games in Milwaukee, including four outs in Game 2, and he has four strikeouts in 2 1/3 innings.
Asked what his plan was for the back end of the bullpen, including closer Trevor Megill, Brewers manager Pat Murphy said on Tuesday's off day at Dodger Stadium, "Keep throwing them out there. They can rest next year."
After a beat, Murphy added, "Familiarity to a team is a thing. You have to be conscious of that too. We're not going to go forward without other people stepping up. Some other people have to step up."
So far the Brewers have used six pitchers in relief, including starting pitcher Dustin May for an inning in Game 2. The active pitchers Milwaukee hasn't used yet — aside from Game 3 starter Robert Gasser — are right-handers Antonio Senzatela and Chad Patrick, plus left-handers Shane Drohan and Kyle Harrison.

item.content:encoded:
William Contreras se consolida como el mejor bate latino de los playoffs y acerca a Milwaukee a una barrida sobre los Dodgers.
William Contreras llegó a esta postemporada como una de las piezas centrales de los Milwaukee Brewers, pero su producción está superando incluso las previsiones más optimistas. El receptor venezolano respondió en los turnos de mayor presión y se convirtió en el bate latino más productivo de estos playoffs, con una combinación de contacto, poder y capacidad para impulsar carreras.
Su actuación más reciente confirmó ese momento. Contreras conectó un jonrón de 436 pies en el quinto inning del segundo juego de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional y empató la pizarra 4-4 ante los Dodgers. Una entrada después, pegó el sencillo que produjo la carrera de la ventaja definitiva en la victoria 7-4 de Milwaukee.
Ese resultado permitió que los Brewers pusieran 2-0 la serie antes del viaje a Los Ángeles. Contreras terminó el encuentro con tres hits en cuatro turnos, tres carreras impulsadas y una base por bolas. Cada uno de sus imparables produjo el empate o puso a Milwaukee adelante.
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Pagés, Chourio, Contreras y Díaz: cuatro historias rumbo a la Serie Mundial
¿Qué números tiene William Contreras en estos playoffs?
El venezolano registra promedio de .391, tres jonrones, cinco carreras impulsadas y cuatro anotadas en 23 turnos al bate. También suma nueve hits, cuatro boletos, porcentaje de embasado de .481, slugging de .783 y OPS de 1.264 durante seis partidos.
Su promedio lo ubica en el cuarto lugar entre todos los bateadores de MLB en esta postemporada. Los tres jugadores que aparecen por encima son Nico Hoerner, Ben Rice y Michael Harris II, por lo cual Contreras ocupa el primer puesto entre los peloteros latinoamericanos.
La cifra también refleja un salto importante frente a su rendimiento durante la campaña regular. Contreras cerró esa etapa con promedio de .270, 18 cuadrangulares y 94 impulsadas en 147 juegos. En octubre elevó su promedio 121 puntos y mantuvo una producción de poder mucho más alta en un momento decisivo de la temporada.
Ese contraste explica por qué su desempeño supera lo que podía anticiparse a partir de sus números de temporada. El catcher no solo acumula hits. También los consigue en situaciones que modifican el rumbo de los partidos.
¿Por qué Contreras es el mejor bate de Milwaukee?
Contreras lidera a los bateadores regulares de Milwaukee en promedio, jonrones y OPS durante esta postemporada. Sus tres cuadrangulares representan el 60% de los cinco que acumula el equipo, mientras su promedio de .391 supera el .368 de Christian Yelich.
Los números adquieren más valor por su puesto. El venezolano cumple las exigencias defensivas de la receptoría y mantiene presencia constante en el corazón del lineup. Durante la temporada regular lideró a los catchers de las Grandes Ligas en entradas detrás del plato y fijó una marca de la franquicia con 89 carreras impulsadas mientras actuó como receptor.
Milwaukee también necesita su capacidad para alargar turnos. Contreras solo suma tres ponches en 27 apariciones al plato y recibió cuatro boletos. Ese control de la zona le permite alcanzar una base con frecuencia y evita que los lanzadores rivales encuentren salidas sencillas en la parte fuerte del orden ofensivo.
Contreras es ahora mismo el mejor bate de los Brewers porque combina promedio, poder y producción en momentos clave. Su impacto no depende de una sola actuación. El venezolano ya conectó tres jonrones y alcanzó base en 13 de sus 27 visitas al plato.
¿Qué necesita Milwaukee para barrer a los Dodgers?
La serie regresará a Los Ángeles con los Brewers a dos victorias del título de la Liga Nacional. Milwaukee tendrá la oportunidad de completar la barrida si gana los próximos dos encuentros en Dodger Stadium.
El cambio de sede aumentará la exigencia para una alineación que hasta ahora encontró respuestas oportunas. Los Dodgers cuentan con profundidad en su cuerpo de lanzadores y tendrán el respaldo de su público, pero llegan al tercer juego después de perder los dos primeros choques de la serie.
Milwaukee necesita que Contreras conserve su disciplina y su capacidad para castigar lanzamientos en la zona. Su bate puede marcar la diferencia frente a un rival que no ofrece mucho margen, en especial si los juegos vuelven a llegar cerrados a los innings finales.
Los Brewers también requerirán apoyo del resto de la ofensiva y en este escenario ChristianYelich (.368) luce como otro nombre clave pues el bateador designado batea por encima de .300. Si el venezolano mantiene este nivel, Milwaukee contará con una opción real de barrer a los Dodgers en California y asegurar su boleto a la Serie Mundial.

Los Milwaukee Brewers aprovecharon los errores y las oportunidades ofensivas para vencer 7-4 a Los Angeles Dodgers en el segundo juego de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional. Con 12 imparables, los locales remontaron en distintos momentos del encuentro y tomaron una ventaja de 2-0 en la serie.
Vinny Castilla elogia a Jonathan Aranda por su actuación con Tampa Bay en los playoffs de MLB
El conjunto angelino llegó a ponerse al frente en tres ocasiones, pero no consiguió contener la respuesta de Milwaukee. Los Dodgers encontraron carreras en la primera, tercera y quinta entradas; sin embargo, los Brewers respondieron con batazos oportunos para cambiar el partido.
William Contreras y Brice Turang lideraron el ataque de Milwaukee
William Contreras fue una de las grandes figuras de la tarde al terminar con tres imparables y tres carreras impulsadas, incluido un cuadrangular en la quinta entrada. El receptor conectó también sencillos productores en el primer y sexto episodios para mantener a su equipo en la pelea.
Brice Turang también tuvo una actuación determinante, con tres carreras anotadas y una impulsada. Christian Yelich produjo dos carreras con un sencillo en la tercera entrada, mientras Jake Bauers contribuyó con un imparable productor en el octavo episodio para ampliar la ventaja de los Brewers
JoJo Romero se queda con la victoria; Brock Stewart carga con la derrota
El mexicano-estadounidense JoJo Romero se acreditó la victoria, mientras que Brock Stewart fue el pitcher derrotado y Aaron Ashby consiguió el salvamento. Milwaukee encontró la manera de inclinar el encuentro a su favor y cerró la novena entrada sin permitir una reacción de los Dodgers.
Los Brewers aseguraron el triunfo con dos carreras en la octava entrada, cuando Turang conectó un sencillo productor y Bauers agregó otro imparable que permitió anotar una carrera más.
Ahora, la serie se trasladará a Los Ángeles para el tercer encuentro, programado para el miércoles 14 de octubre, donde los Dodgers estarán obligados a reaccionar si quieren mantenerse con vida en la pelea por el campeonato de la Liga Nacional.

If Boston Red Sox fans are still watching the Major League Baseball postseason, they're probably picking up on some reasons their team didn't make it this far.
Though the Red Sox had one magical stretch of 32-5 baseball this season, it was painfully obvious by the time they finished their Wild Card Series at Yankee Stadium that they were never built for a deep playoff run. And the way their offense functioned in that series was a microcosm of the season.
When the chips were on the table, the Red Sox couldn't put anyone next to Willson Contreras in the lineup that was capable of inflicting damage. Even with a bum hand, Contreras hit well enough in that series to help the team move on — it was just that all of his teammates failed to rise to the task.
Red Sox fall short of other lineup cores
The teams still playing all have some sort of dynamic duo, trio, or better in their lineup. The Milwaukee Brewers have Jackson Chourio, Brice Turang, and William Contreras. The Los Angeles Dodgers have the most star-studded lineup we've ever seen, with $60 million man Kyle Tucker batting eighth.
The Tampa Bay Rays have Yandy Díaz and Jonathan Aranda providing thump in front of Junior Caminero. Even the Cleveland Guardians have a strong supporting cast around José Ramírez, with Steven Kwan getting on base, Jo Adell driving balls in the gap, and Chase DeLauter lurking.
But in the Wild Card Series, as soon as it was clear that Roman Anthony's hand was toast, the Red Sox had no other threats in front of or behind Contreras. Adley Rutschman's at-bats got worse as the series went along, while Wilyer Abreu and Ceddanne Rafaela looked absolutely lost in the batter's box.
There's a lesson to be learned here. Even if the Red Sox feel good about the steps forward some of their hitters can take from this season into next, it seems imperative at this point to add another star-caliber bat. And that's not going to be easy, given the impending lockout and soft free agency class.
Whether it's buying high on Randy Arozarena or further depleting the farm system for Hunter Goodman, the Red Sox are going to have to do something uncomfortable to give themselves a real shot at contention.

MILWAUKEE -- Tarik Skubal has been about as consistent as they come since being traded to the Dodgers this summer, but for the first time in eight postseason starts, the two-time Cy Young Award winner did not record an out beyond the fifth inning.
In a highly anticipated matchup between two of the most dominant starters in baseball, the Dodgers fell to the Brewers, 2-1, after Skubal allowed two runs over five innings in Game 1 of the NL Championship Series on Sunday night at American Family Field.
The Dodgers were able to chase the Brewers' Jacob Misiorowski -- this year's presumptive NL Cy Young Award winner -- with one out in the fifth inning, but Andy Pages' RBI single in the second was the only damage they managed against him.
It was a tale of two trips through the order for Skubal, who was dominant through his first three innings. He retired nine of the first 10 Brewers he faced, striking out six of them. Andrew Vaughn, who doubled in the second inning, was the lone baserunner he allowed in that span.
But the Brewers came to life when they saw him for a second time. To open the fourth inning, Skubal fell behind 2-0 to Brice Turang, then tried to get back in the count by painting the inside corner with a sinker. Turang launched the offering a Statcast-projected 384 feet to left-center, out of reach of center fielder Pages, to tie the game.
Skubal's command began to falter in the fifth inning, when he issued a leadoff walk to Garrett Mitchell. Gifted a free base, the Brewers played their style of baseball to take the lead. Cooper Pratt bunted Mitchell over to second, and Mitchell scored on a base hit up the middle from Luis Lara.
The Brewers loaded the bases on a Jackson Chourio single and a Turang walk, but Skubal was able to get William Contreras to fly out to escape the jam. Still, the stressful fifth inning raised Skubal's pitch count to 81, and he was lifted in favor of Alex Vesia for the sixth.

Dodgers make Tarik Skubal decision that should worry Brewers before NLCS showdown originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Los Angeles Dodgers are four victories away from returning to the World Series, and manager Dave Roberts has revealed how his team plans to attack the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Championship Series.
Roberts announced Friday that Tarik Skubal will start Game 1 on Sunday, with Yoshinobu Yamamoto scheduled to pitch Game 2 on Monday. The decision gives Los Angeles two of baseball's most accomplished pitchers to begin a series that features the National League's top two regular-season teams.
The announcement also provides another reminder of the extraordinary pitching depth the Dodgers have assembled. Los Angeles is attempting to win its third consecutive World Series championship, and its starting rotation could become the biggest obstacle standing between Milwaukee and its own championship ambitions.
Tarik Skubal gets another opportunity to set the tone
Skubal will take the mound Sunday at American Family Field after delivering an excellent performance against the Atlanta Braves in the Division Series. The two-time Cy Young Award winner allowed one run on two hits over six innings in Game 1, striking out seven batters while issuing two walks.
Tarik Skubal will start Game 1 with Yoshinobu Yamamoto starting Game 2 for the Dodgers in the NLCS against the Brewers, per @ByJackHarris https://t.co/e8wI91D6uF
— Talkin' Baseball (@TalkinBaseball_) October 9, 2026
Los Angeles acquired Skubal from the Detroit Tigers in a blockbuster August trade, adding another established ace to an already talented pitching staff. His arrival strengthened a rotation that included Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow, giving Roberts multiple options capable of controlling a postseason game.
Starting Skubal in Game 1 is an important decision because Milwaukee owns home-field advantage in the series. The Brewers finished the regular season with 103 victories, while the Dodgers reached the 100-win mark. A strong opening performance would allow Los Angeles to immediately put pressure on a team that has been extremely difficult to beat throughout the year.
Skubal's ability to limit baserunners and generate strikeouts could be particularly valuable against a Milwaukee lineup featuring Christian Yelich, Jackson Chourio and William Contreras.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto gives Dodgers another major advantage
Yamamoto will follow Skubal in Game 2 after producing one of the Dodgers' best pitching performances against Atlanta. The right-hander struck out 10 batters over seven innings, allowing only one run on four hits in a victory that helped Los Angeles regain control of the Division Series.
The performance continued an impressive postseason history for Yamamoto, who earned World Series MVP honors in 2025. His ability to deliver deep, efficient outings gives Roberts another dependable option before the series shifts to Dodger Stadium. Milwaukee is expected to rely heavily on its own talented young pitchers, including Jacob Misiorowski and Logan Henderson. The Brewers have demonstrated throughout the season that they can compete with baseball's most talented rosters, but matching Los Angeles on the mound will be a significant challenge.
The Dodgers also have decisions remaining beyond their first two starters. Roberts indicated Friday that the team was considering adding another pitcher to its NLCS roster, a move that would require removing a position player.
Dodgers still have questions despite pitching advantage
One concern involves veteran utility player Miguel Rojas, who left Game 3 against Atlanta because of lower back discomfort. Rojas participated in baseball activities Friday, but Roberts stopped short of confirming his availability for the championship series.
The Dodgers eliminated Atlanta in four games, while Milwaukee also advanced with a four-game victory over San Diego. The teams now meet in the NLCS for the second consecutive postseason, creating another opportunity for the Brewers to challenge the defending champions. Game 1 is scheduled for Sunday at 8 p.m. ET, with Game 2 following Monday at 5 p.m. ET.
Los Angeles has plenty of offensive talent, including Shohei Ohtani, but its starting pitching could determine how this series unfolds. By sending Skubal and Yamamoto to the mound in Milwaukee, Roberts is giving the Dodgers an opportunity to establish control before returning home.

New York Yankees impending free-agent first baseman/designated hitter Paul Goldschmidt has expressed a desire to keep playing at age 39 in 2027, according to Gary Phillips of the New York Daily News. It is unclear if the Yankees will make an effort to re-sign the former MVP and seven-time All-Star in the offseason. Goldy had a nice bounce-back campaign in 2026 in his 16th year in the big leagues after he hit just 10 homers and drove in 45 runs in 146 games in 2025 in his first year in pinstripes. In 105 regular-season games across 380 plate appearances this year, Goldschmidt hit .252/.313/.452 with a .765 OPS, 18 home runs, 52 RBI, and 44 runs scored for the Yankees. He went hitless in eight plate appearances with two walks and a run scored in four postseason games for New York this year. Goldschmidt is obviously no longer in his prime and is no longer an everyday player, but he should still attract interest across the league for his ability to hit lefties. In 183 plate appearances against southpaws in 2026, he hit .299 (47-for-157) with 11 of his 18 home runs and 24 RBI.--Keith Hernandez

Across 660 regular-season plate appearances split between the Guardians and the Los Angeles Angels, Adell hit .240/.298/.401 with 23 home runs, 94 RBI, 70 runs scored, and five stolen bases. Oct 7, 2026, 9:19 PM ET

Keith Hernandez

One of the New York Yankees prime trade deadline needs was believed to be the catcher position. It seemed like a foregone conclusion that the club would target help behind the plate, as Austin Wells struggled miserably throughout the first half of the season. Brian Cashman seemed to feel otherwise.
Wells rebounded somewhat in the second half, hitting .229/.351/.436 down the stretch. Still, the Yankees might not want to roll into 2026 with Wells, or at least might be wary of counting on him as the primary catcher moving forward. There will be options in free agency, highlighted by Ryan Jeffers, but after him there's Tyler Stephenson and a bunch of questionable options. The bidding for Jeffers could get hot, so New York might turn to the trade market to scratch its itch behind the dish.
That could bring a risky trade partner back into the fold: the Milwaukee Brewers, who could find themselves dangling William Contreras in order to bring back a haul.
Trading the soon-to-be 29-year-old would follow the Brewers' M.O. He'll be entering his final year of team control in 2027, and his last two seasons have been good, but a downgrade from his peak in 2023 through 2024. This season, Contreras hit .270/.341/.417 with 18 homers, which is good production regardless of position, but looks even better in light of the fact that he's a catcher
| William Contreras fWAR by year since becoming a regular |
|---|
| 2023 - 5.8 |
| 2024 - 5.5 |
| 2025 - 3.7 |
| 2026 - 3.0 |
A Yankees-Brewers William Contreras trade would be a Devin Williams type of risk that further ignites Red Sox rivalry
Whether Devin Williams flopped because he was on the decline or because he just didn't want to play in New York is unclear, but Milwaukee has a history of fleecing people in these kinds of trades. Just look at what they did to the Mets with Freddy Peralta for further proof.
There's a real reason to engage the Brewers with caution, even for an offensive force at catcher like Contreras. However, if Brian Cashman made a move for the backstop, he'd be throwing even more gas on the Yankees' never-ending rivalry with the Boston Red Sox.
The Red Sox employ William's older brother, Willson Contreras, so such a move would add a sibling rivalry dynamic to the competition between these long-standing enemies. Willson is fiery player, who has both taken Boston's leadership to task while also threatening to use his no-trade clause if the Red Sox approached him about a trade prior to Boston's turn of fortune ahead of the deadline.
William is an equally passionate player, following in his older brother's footsteps with stirring displays of emotion on the field. Putting the two of them together, on opposite sides of the most heated rivalry in sports, would create a highly combustible situation that could be a lot of fun to watch.
It's all speculation for now. The Brewers have shown no indication that they'd want to trade Contreras, and we'd have to admit that while he'd be an intriguing option, we'd be wary if they actively shopped him. At the same time, if he landed in pinstripes and it worked out, next year's Yankees-Red Sox matchups could be full of fireworks and a lot of fun.

The Milwaukee Brewers have a certain style of play and they aren't going to stray from it, even in a franchise history-making win.
On Thursday, Milwaukee won its 100th game of the season, which is the first time in franchise history that a club has reached triple digits, and the Brewers clinched the No. 1 seed in the National League playoffs at the same time. It was a big night, to say the least. Still, despite everything on the line, Milwaukee didn't change how it handles things. For example, William Contreras — who has been red-hot recently — was benched in the eighth inning with the score knotted at one for not running out a grounder earlier in the game.
Jackson Chourio pinch-hit for Contreras and after the game, Brewers manager Pat Murphy confirmed the reason for the All-Star backstop being pulled, as transcribed by Brewers broadcaster Dominic Cotroneo of 620 WTMJ.
The Brewers Play The Game The Right Way
"He didn't run the ball out and [Trea Turner] muffed it," Cotroneo wrote. "I didn't know whether he was gonna be safe. Everyone knows how much William does for our team, how hard he plays, how much he competes. ... But we don't accept that, and he knows that."
The Brewers play the game the right way, and this is yet another example of how. With win No. 100 and the No. 1 seed in the National League on the line, Milwaukee stuck with the precedent it has had all season. Back in August, Brewers shortstop Cooper Pratt was benched in a game for the same thing. He didn't run hard out of the box on a ball that dropped in and got a single, rather than a double.
In Contreras' case, he has been one of the hottest hitters in Milwaukee's lineup recently. Since Aug. 27, he has been slashing .282/.354/.565 with a .918 OPS, six home runs, 28 RBIs, 11 walks, and six doubles. He has been elite and is a big reason why the Brewers were in the position they were in to clinch. That's why it's even more important that the Brewers handled the situation the same way as with the rookie.
They have set the tone and whether you're a multi-time All-Star or a rookie finding your way, in Milwaukee everyone is held to the same standards. It's a good practice to have in professional sports. Plus, it doesn't hurt that Chourio came in and walked, stole a base and then eventually blasted his 25th homer of the season. That makes the decision look a little better, to say the least. The Brewers play the game the right way and were rewarded for it.

item.content:encoded:
PHILADELPHIA -- Even on the night his team became the first in the Majors in three years to win 100 games, Brewers manager Pat Murphy showed he still has the pedal to the metal.
Murphy pulled one of his best players, All-Star catcher William Contreras, for a pinch-hitter in the eighth inning of Milwaukee’s 5-1 win over the Phillies on Thursday night at Citizens Bank Park. It proved to be the right move, because pinch-hitter Jackson Chourio responded by working a walk, stealing second base and scoring the go-ahead run.
But it was also Murphy sending a message. Contreras had not run hard on a groundout to shortstop Trea Turner in the fifth inning. Turner bobbled the baseball, but still had plenty of time to throw to first for the inning-ending out in a tie game.
“I don’t know if he could have been safe or not,” Murphy said. “Everybody knows how much William does for our team, how hard he plays and how much he competes. But he’s also a guy that people expect a lot out of. We don’t accept that. He knows that.”
It’s not uncommon for Contreras to pick his moments to run hard, and the Brewers generally don’t mind that he does. He’s played at least 141 games and started at least 108 games behind the plate in each of his four seasons with the Brewers, and is the first catcher in Brewers history to catch at least 1,000 innings in three straight seasons. His 1,074 2/3 innings behind the plate this season are most in the Majors.
“There’s never going to be a time when you’re not responsible for playing winning baseball,” Murphy said. “It’s a guy that has done so much for the Brewers, he still has to abide by all the same [rules]. He doesn’t have to go 100 percent every time down the baseline, but when a guy muffs it, you have to be going hard enough that you’re safe if he does muff it.
“That’s winning baseball. Because that at-bat is important. Because every one of those at-bats is important.”
How did Murphy’s move land in the clubhouse?
“I think it’s great. I’m sure you guys have heard him say it because he says it to us all the time: ‘You can’t coast uphill,’” said first baseman Jake Bauers, who supplied Thursday night’s winning hit. “He wants [us] to keep [our] foot on the gas. We want to keep the foot on the gas. And we don’t want to go into the postseason feeling like we already did something. It’s really just, keep our heads down, keep working, keep preparing and go out and execute at a high clip.”
To be fair, Contreras was not the only player who raised Murphy’s ire. Yes, the Brewers won their 100th game in a season for the first time in club history. Yes, they completed a 7-2 final road trip in which they won every series and clinched the division, the best record in franchise history and a first-round bye in the postseason.
But a manager always sees ways his team can be better.
“Out of the 30 teams, very few over the next 10 years will win 100,” Murphy said. “I’m just grateful and proud to be a part of it, truly. And I’m proud we have this group of guys. Now, did we play great baseball tonight? No. Have we been playing great baseball? No. The strikeouts are concerning offensively.
“But, the guys, they like being together and they like this winning thing. They can’t take it for granted, because it’s special. But you have to put in the work to do it.”

The Milwaukee Brewers have a 100-win season. With a victory over the Philadelphia Phillies on Thursday night, the 2026 Brew Crew improved to 100-59 on the 2026 season, reaching an unbelievable milestone that hadn't been accomplished in the first 57 seasons of the franchise's history.
After projection models expected the Brewers to finish with somewhere between 80-85 wins during the 2026 season, Pat Murphy's squad has proved the preseason predictions wrong once again. However, they didn't just surpass their expected win total by a few games; they blew past the projections, produced the best regular season in franchise history, and reached the elusive 100-win mark.
It's an unbelievable accomplishment, one that is made even more impressive by the fact that Milwaukee has produced 90+ win seasons in each of the last four seasons and five times in the last six years. This isn't a one-off season in which the Brewers sacrificed their future and went "all in" on one year. Rather, it's just another chapter in what has easily been the most successful stretch of seasons in franchise history. Put another way, to win 100 games with the best farm system in baseball makes the achievement that much more incredible.
It took a pair of wins over the Philadelphia Phillies, who still have plenty to play for, to achieve 100 wins before their final series of the regular season. With the Brewers fully in postseason preparation mode, made clear by a number of roster and in-game decisions, Murphy's team displayed their impressive depth in their late-September series victory over the Phillies. Said roster depth will be key in the postseason.
Brewers' rely on impressive roster depth to reach elusive 100-win mark after postseason preparation has begun
The Brewers entered Thursday night's series finale against the Phillies with a first-round bye, and therefore a spot in the NLDS, already secured. They didn't have nearly as much to play for as Philadelphia, who is fighting to secure home-field advantage in the Wild Card Series. As a result, Murphy turned to Shane Drohan, who is expected to be a reliever in October, for a short start, didn't include Christian Yelich or Jackson Chourio in the starting lineup, and opted to have William Contreras DH during the series finale on Thursday night. Murphy didn't use Abner Uribe or Trevor Megill and kept Antonio Senzatela in for a save in the ninth inning, and yet, even with their postseason preparation fully underway, the Brewers knocked off the mighty Phillies, who have not officially clinched a spot in the postseason just yet.
In other words, the Brewers won their 100th game of the season on Thursday night due to their impressive roster depth. Murphy's squad proved that they can defeat a postseason team like the Phillies without using one of their top starters, without starting Chourio or Yelich, and without turning to their elite high-leverage duo at the end of the ballgame.
That type of roster depth bodes well for Milwaukee's chances in October. A deep postseason run, like the one the Brewers are hoping to put together, requires contributions throughout the roster. Whether it be a pinch-hit appearance, escaping a jam in the middle innings, or serving as a defensive replacement late in the game, the 26 Brewers that Milwaukee elects to include on their postseason roster will each have their role. It's therefore encouraging to see so many of them contribute to the Brewers' late-season series win over the Phillies, which led to 100 wins.
The Brewers have three games left to improve their record-breaking regular season record even further. Expect a similar strategy, in which Murphy relies on his depth to give necessary rest to each of his players, in the Brewers' upcoming weekend series against the St. Louis Cardinals. That said, regardless of how the final series plays out, the 2026 Brewers officially have a 100-win season to their name -- a truly incredible accomplishment.
